# splunkctl documentation

> splunkctl is a CLI and MCP server for operating Splunk Enterprise, Enterprise Security, and Splunk SOAR with guarded, previewable changes.

Each section below is one page of https://splunkctl.danny.vn, linked by its source URL.
The generated command reference is kept separate: browse https://splunkctl.danny.vn/#/commands/README
(raw: https://splunkctl.danny.vn/commands/README.md) or load https://splunkctl.danny.vn/commands.json for the
machine-readable command tree. Index: https://splunkctl.danny.vn/llms.txt

## splunkctl

Source: https://splunkctl.danny.vn/README.md


Operate Splunk Enterprise, Enterprise Security, and Splunk SOAR from a terminal, or give an AI agent the same commands through MCP.

Requires Python 3.12+ and credentials for your Splunk instance. splunkctl is an independent community project, not affiliated with or endorsed by Splunk Inc.

### Quickstart

```bash
python -m pip install splunkctl
splunkctl config init
splunkctl doctor
```

`config init` writes `~/.splunkctl/config.yaml`. `doctor` checks the connection, authentication, server health, and your permissions. See [Install](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/install.md) for shell completion, and [Configure](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/configure.md) for profiles and environment variables.

### Safety

Every command that changes a remote Splunk or SOAR instance previews by default and exits without changing anything; some previews read the current state first to show a diff. The preview names the target host, and the active profile for Splunk Enterprise. Add `--yes` to apply. `state push --report FILE` writes a change report you can attach to a change ticket. Local configuration writes (`config init`, `config use`, `auth login`, `mcp install`) are not guarded.

### Investigate

Run SPL, read fired alerts, and triage Enterprise Security notables without leaving the terminal.

- [Run searches](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/search.md)
- [Review fired alerts](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/alerts.md)
- [Triage ES notables](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/es.md)
- [Manage dashboards](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/dashboards.md)

### Detect

Keep detections, knowledge objects, and parsing configuration in version control and deploy them across instances.

## Install

Source: https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/install.md


When to use: you are putting splunkctl on a workstation, a jump host, or a CI runner for the first time, or adding an optional component to an existing install.

### Prerequisites

- Python 3.12 or newer with `pip`.
- Network access from this machine to the Splunk REST API (port 8089 by default) and, for SOAR, to the SOAR REST port (8443 by default).
- A Splunk account. `splunkctl doctor` reports which permissions it has; each command needs the capabilities its action requires.

### Synopsis

```text
python -m pip install splunkctl
python -m pip install 'splunkctl[browser]'
python -m pip install git+https://github.com/dannyota/splunk-sdk-python@splunkctl
splunkctl --version
splunkctl config init [--profile NAME] [--soar]
splunkctl doctor [--strict]
splunkctl completion <bash|zsh|fish>
```

### Workflow

#### Install from PyPI

```bash
python -m pip install splunkctl
splunkctl --version
```

Expected result: `splunkctl, version X.Y.Z`. If the output looks different, Splunk's own `splunkctl` binary is ahead of this package on your `PATH`; run `splunkctl-py` instead (see [Relationship to Splunk's splunkctl](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/splunk-cli.md)).

Core commands work with the upstream Splunk SDK that `pip` installs as a dependency.

#### Add optional components

Browser SAML login (`splunkctl auth login`) needs Playwright:

```bash
python -m pip install 'splunkctl[browser]'
```

See [Log in through browser SAML](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/auth.md) for the browser setup that follows.

#### Install from source

```bash
git clone https://github.com/dannyota/splunkctl.git
cd splunkctl
python -m pip install -e .
```

For a development install with test tooling, see [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/dannyota/splunkctl/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md).

#### Configure and verify

```bash
splunkctl config init
splunkctl doctor
```

`config init` prompts for host, port, username, and password and writes `~/.splunkctl/config.yaml` on this machine (not guarded). `doctor` checks the connection, authentication, server health, and your permissions. Expected result: every check passes; `--strict` turns warnings into exit 1 for CI. Add SOAR afterwards with `splunkctl config init --soar` and `splunkctl soar test`. Profiles and environment variables are covered in [Configure](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/configure.md).

#### Enable shell completion

Add the matching line to your shell profile, then restart the shell or source the file.

Bash (`~/.bashrc`):

```bash
eval "$(splunkctl completion bash)"
```

Zsh (`~/.zshrc`):

```bash
eval "$(splunkctl completion zsh)"
```

Fish (`~/.config/fish/config.fish`):

```bash
splunkctl completion fish | source
```

### Troubleshooting

- `pip` reports no matching distribution: your Python is older than 3.12. Check with `python --version` and install a newer interpreter.
- `splunkctl --version` prints something other than `splunkctl, version X.Y.Z`: another `splunkctl` is first on `PATH`; use `splunkctl-py`.
- `doctor` fails on connection: confirm host and port, and that the REST port is reachable from this machine (`curl -k https://HOST:8089/services/server/info`).
- `doctor` reports a Splunk-format config file: `~/.splunkctl/config.yaml` belongs to Splunk's CLI; run `splunkctl config init --path ~/.splunkctl/profiles.yaml` or see [Relationship to Splunk's splunkctl](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/splunk-cli.md).

### See also

- [Configure](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/configure.md)
- [Diagnose a connection](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/doctor.md)
- [Set up the MCP server](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/mcp.md)
- [Relationship to Splunk's splunkctl](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/splunk-cli.md)

## Configure

Source: https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/configure.md


When to use: splunkctl is installed and you need to point it at one or more Splunk instances, choose how credentials are supplied, and switch between development, UAT, and production without mutating the wrong host.

### Prerequisites

- splunkctl installed (see [Install](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/install.md)).
- The host, management port (8089 by default), and either a bearer token or a username and password for each instance.
- For SOAR, the SOAR host, REST port (8443 by default), and automation token; see [Set up and check SOAR](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/soar.md).

### Synopsis

```text
splunkctl config init [--host HOST] [--port PORT] [--username USER] [--password PASS] [--scheme https|http] [--verify|--no-verify] [--profile NAME] [--path FILE] [--web-url URL] [--auth-mode auto|token|password|browser]
splunkctl config init --soar [--sso-url URL] [--profile NAME]
splunkctl config show
splunkctl config use <NAME>
splunkctl config test
splunkctl --profile <NAME> <COMMAND>
splunkctl --config <FILE> <COMMAND>
splunkctl --watch <SECONDS> <READ_ONLY_COMMAND>
```

### Workflow

#### Run interactive setup

```bash
splunkctl config init
splunkctl config test
```

Expected result: `config init` prompts for host (default `localhost`), port (8089), username (`admin`), password, and TLS verification (default yes), then writes `~/.splunkctl/config.yaml` with `0600` permissions and prints `Config saved to ...`. Every prompt can be answered with the matching flag instead. SAML detection runs only when `--web-url URL` is supplied (see [Log in through browser SAML](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/auth.md)). `config test` connects, authenticates, and prints the server name and version.

#### Write the config file by hand

The file is `~/.splunkctl/config.yaml`:

```yaml
host: "localhost"
port: 8089
scheme: "https"
username: "admin"
password: ""            # optional, can use token instead
token: ""               # bearer token (preferred)
verify: true            # TLS cert verification (default: on)
app: "search"           # default app context
owner: "nobody"         # default owner context
```

TLS verification is on by default, so production instances with valid certificates work out of the box. For lab instances with self-signed certificates set `verify: false` explicitly; `config init` asks during setup.

#### Add profiles for dev, UAT, and prod

For more than one instance, add a `profiles:` map and a `current:` pointer instead of the flat keys:

```yaml
profiles:
  dev:
    host: "dev.splunk.internal"
    username: "admin"
    password: "devpass"
  uat:
    host: "uat.splunk.internal"
    token: "..."
  prod:
    host: "prod.splunk.internal"
    token: "..."
current: "uat"           # active profile when nothing else selects one
```

```bash
splunkctl config init --profile uat
splunkctl config use uat
splunkctl config show
splunkctl --profile prod config show
splunkctl --profile prod rules list
```

Expected result: `config init --profile NAME` creates or updates one named profile; `config use` points `current` at it without a connectivity test; `config show` prints the active profile with secrets redacted plus the other profile names; the global `--profile` flag overrides the pointer for one invocation. Selection precedence: `--profile <name>` > `current:` pointer > `default`.

Legacy files keep working. A flat file (no `profiles:` key) is treated as an implicit profile named `default`, nothing to migrate. Bare `config init` writes that flat shape, unless the destination already has a `profiles:` key, in which case it folds the new values into `profiles.default` and leaves sibling profiles and `current` untouched, so it never clobbers a multi-profile file. The first `config init --profile <name>` against a legacy file upgrades it in place: the old flat keys move under `profiles.default`, the new profile is added beside it, and permissions stay `0600`.

Every dry-run preview and `--yes` confirmation prints which instance is about to be mutated, for example `[DRY RUN] Create index 'x' (profile: uat @ uat.splunk.internal:8089)`, so switching between dev, UAT, and prod never happens silently. The banner is built from local config only; it never opens a connection.

#### Override with environment variables

| Variable | Maps to |
|---|---|
| `SPLUNK_HOST` | `host` |
| `SPLUNK_PORT` | `port` |
| `SPLUNK_TOKEN` | `token` |
| `SPLUNK_USER` | `username` |
| `SPLUNK_PASS` | `password` |
| `SPLUNK_VERIFY` | `verify` |

`SOAR_HOST`, `SOAR_PORT`, `SOAR_TOKEN`, `SOAR_USER`, `SOAR_PASS`, and `SOAR_VERIFY` override the profile's `soar:` section the same way.

```bash
SPLUNK_HOST=ci.splunk.internal SPLUNK_TOKEN="$CI_TOKEN" splunkctl doctor
```

Resolution order, highest first: CLI flags, environment variables, the selected profile, built-in defaults. `--profile` and `--config` are the only root options that select configuration.

#### Coexist with Splunk's own splunkctl

Splunk's Go CLI, [`splunk/splunkctl`](https://github.com/splunk/splunkctl), also writes `~/.splunkctl/config.yaml`, as a flat file with `host` (a full URL) and `token`. This tool never rewrites that file:

- When `~/.splunkctl/config.yaml` is in Splunk's format and no `--config` is given, this tool reads and writes `~/.splunkctl/profiles.yaml` instead and prints one notice on standard error: `Splunk-format config at ~/.splunkctl/config.yaml; using ~/.splunkctl/profiles.yaml`.
- `splunkctl config init` writes to the same fallback file, so one `config init` is enough on a host that already has Splunk's tool.
- An explicit `--config FILE` is never redirected. If that file is in Splunk's format the command fails with `Splunk-format config at FILE: this is a flat host/token file written by Splunk's splunkctl. Pass a profiles file with --config, or create one with: splunkctl config init --path FILE`.
- `splunkctl doctor` reports the config file in use as its first check.
- A hand-written file in this tool's own legacy flat format that contains only `host` and `token` is indistinguishable from Splunk's format and is treated the same way. Add `port` or `scheme`, or run `config init`, to keep using it.

Both tools install an executable named `splunkctl`. This package also installs `splunkctl-py`, which runs the same CLI, for hosts where Splunk's binary comes first on `PATH`.

#### Watch a read-only command

```bash
splunkctl --watch 5 indexes list
splunkctl --watch 10 server health
splunkctl --watch 3 rules list --filter brute
```

Expected result: the command re-runs every N seconds, clearing the screen between runs like `watch(1)`. Errors are printed in place and the loop continues; Ctrl-C stops it. `--watch` requires an interactive terminal (TTY) and rejects mutation commands (those guarded by `--yes`).

#### Verify

```bash
splunkctl config show
splunkctl config test
splunkctl doctor
```

Expected result: the active profile with secrets redacted, a successful connection and login, and a passing check list.

### Troubleshooting

- `config` error or `Config` check failing in `doctor`: the YAML is not a mapping or is unreadable; fix the file or pass `--config FILE`.
- `Splunk-format config at FILE` with `--config`: that file belongs to Splunk's CLI; pass a profiles file or create one with `splunkctl config init --path FILE`.
- A profile-not-found error: the name is not under `profiles:`; check `splunkctl config show` for the known names.
- `auth` from `config test`: wrong token or password for that profile; environment variables such as `SPLUNK_TOKEN` override the file, so unset them when testing a profile.
- `connection` from `config test`: host or port wrong, or the REST port is blocked; `curl -k https://HOST:8089/services/server/info` from this machine.
- TLS certificate error on a lab instance: set `verify: false` in that profile or `SPLUNK_VERIFY=false`.
- `--watch requires an interactive terminal (TTY)` or `--watch cannot be used with mutation commands`: run it in a terminal and only with read-only commands.

## Run searches

Source: https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/search.md


When to use: you want to run SPL against a remote Splunk instance from your terminal for hunting, incident response, or detection tuning, pull large result sets to a file, push a local file into an index, or check on and cancel long-running jobs.

### Prerequisites

- A profile that passes `splunkctl doctor` (see [Configure](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/configure.md)).
- A role with search access to the indexes you query. `upload` needs permission to post data to the `receivers/simple` endpoint.
- Always scope `--earliest`; unscoped searches scan all time.

### Synopsis

```text
splunkctl search run <SPL> [--earliest TIME] [--latest TIME] [--limit N] [--app APP] [--detach] [--yes]
splunkctl search export <SPL> [--earliest TIME] [--latest TIME] [--app APP] [--yes]
splunkctl search oneshot <SPL> [--earliest TIME] [--latest TIME] [--limit N] [--app APP] [--yes]
splunkctl search jobs [--filter SID_SUBSTRING] [--limit N] [--offset N]
splunkctl search job <SID> [--offset N] [--count N] [--events] [--status-only]
splunkctl search cancel <SID> [--yes]
splunkctl search upload --path <FILE> [--index INDEX] [--sourcetype TYPE] [--source TEXT] [--host HOST] [--yes]
splunkctl search metrics --index <INDEX> [--metric NAME] [--filter PREFIX] [--app APP]
```

### Workflow

#### Run an interactive search

```bash
splunkctl search run \
    'index=auth sourcetype=linux_secure "Failed password" | stats count by src_ip | where count > 20' \
    --earliest -24h
splunkctl search run \
    'index=wineventlog EventCode=4625 | stats count by Account_Name, src_ip | where count > 10' \
    --earliest -1d --limit 500
```

Expected result: `run` creates a normal job, polls until it finishes, and prints up to `--limit` rows (default 100). Use it for most interactive work: detection tuning, hunting, triage queries. When more rows exist the output names the sid and the `search job <SID> --offset N` command that fetches the next page.

| Flag | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `--earliest` | none | Splunk time syntax: `-1h`, `-7d@d`, `2025-01-15T00:00:00` |
| `--latest` | `now` | Use `@d` to snap to midnight boundaries |
| `--limit` | 100 | Max rows returned (`run` and `oneshot` only; `export` has no cap) |
| `--app` | none | App namespace context (for example `SplunkEnterpriseSecuritySuite`) |

Time-range tips: snap-to modifiers reduce bucket scanning (`-1d@d` is yesterday midnight, `-1h@h` the top of the previous hour). For exports over days or weeks, break the range into daily chunks to avoid timeouts on heavy indexes.

Bare keywords get `search` prepended automatically. Pipe-leading queries and generating commands (`makeresults`, `inputlookup`, `tstats`, and others) pass through unchanged.

#### Export a large result set

```bash
splunkctl search export \
    'index=dns query="*.evil-domain.com" | table _time src_ip query answer' \
    --earliest -7d | jq . > dns_hits.json
```

Expected result: results stream to stdout without a job artifact and without a row cap. Use it for bulk extraction, for example a week of firewall logs for offline analysis.

#### Get a quick count

```bash
splunkctl search oneshot 'index=main | stats count' --earliest '@d'
```

Expected result: the fastest path for small, read-only queries: no job object and no poll loop. Good for counts, stats, and quick checks.

#### Run SPL that writes

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host in the active profile. Impact: write commands such as `outputlookup` and `collect` change lookups or indexes on the instance. Preview by running the command without `--yes` and reading the refusal, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with a read search (for example `| inputlookup suspicious_ips.csv`).

```bash
splunkctl search run 'index=auth action=failure | stats count by src_ip | outputlookup suspicious_ips.csv' --earliest -24h
splunkctl search run 'index=auth action=failure | stats count by src_ip | outputlookup suspicious_ips.csv' --earliest -24h --yes
```

Expected result: without `--yes` the first command is refused before dispatch, exits 1, and in JSON output mode (including the non-TTY default) emits a `confirmation_required` error envelope. The refusal covers `outputlookup`, `collect`, `mcollect`, `meventcollect`, `sendalert`, `delete`, `outputcsv`, `outputtext`, `sendemail`, `runshellscript`, and `script`, in `run`, `export`, and `oneshot` alike. With `--yes` the search runs.

#### Manage long-running jobs

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host in the active profile. Impact: `cancel` kills a running job and discards its results. Preview with `splunkctl search cancel 1719648000.12345`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl search jobs --filter 1719648000`.

```bash
splunkctl search run 'index=firewall | tstats count where index=firewall by sourcetype' --earliest -30d --detach
splunkctl search jobs
splunkctl search job 1719648000.12345 --status-only
splunkctl search job 1719648000.12345 --offset 100 --count 100
splunkctl search job 1719648000.12345 --events
splunkctl search cancel 1719648000.12345 --yes
```

Expected result: `--detach` submits the job and prints its sid; `jobs` lists running and recent jobs (`--filter` matches the sid); `job` shows status and pages results (`--count 0` fetches all, `--events` fetches raw events); `cancel` stops it.

#### Upload a local file into an index

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host in the active profile. Impact: the file's lines are indexed as events in `--index` (default `main`) and cannot be unindexed without `delete` rights. Preview with `splunkctl search upload --path iocs.csv --index threat_intel --sourcetype csv`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl search oneshot 'index=threat_intel source="iocs.csv" | stats count'`.

```bash
splunkctl search upload --path iocs.csv --index threat_intel --sourcetype csv --yes
splunkctl search upload --path sample_paloalto.log --index sandbox --sourcetype pan:traffic --yes
splunkctl search upload --path captured.json --index main --host web-prod-03 --yes
```

Expected result: the file is read on your laptop and pushed through the `receivers/simple` REST endpoint; no SSH, shared filesystem, or server-side path is needed. `--sourcetype` is auto-detected when omitted, `--source` defaults to the file name, and `--host` overrides host metadata. Typical uses: a threat-intel CSV (STIX export, OSINT feed) for correlation searches, sample logs from a new vendor to build props and transforms before onboarding the real feed, or captured traffic summaries for analysis.

#### Explore a metrics index

```bash
splunkctl search metrics --index my_metrics
splunkctl search metrics --index my_metrics --filter cpu
splunkctl search metrics --index my_metrics --metric cpu.idle
```

Expected result: all metric names in the index, the names starting with `cpu`, or the dimensions of `cpu.idle`. The command runs `| mcatalog` through `oneshot`, so it needs only search access to the metrics index.

### Troubleshooting

- `confirmation_required` (exit 1): the SPL contains a write command. Add `--yes` only if the write is intended.
- `auth` error: credentials are wrong or the session expired; run `splunkctl doctor`.
- `permission` error on `upload`: the role lacks the capability to post to `receivers/simple`.
- `timeout` on `run`: the job is still running; rerun with `--detach` and poll with `search job <SID> --status-only`, or raise the global `--timeout` (seconds).
- `not_found` on `job` or `cancel`: the sid expired or was typed wrong; list current sids with `splunkctl search jobs`.
- Zero results on a known-good search: check the time range first, then confirm the indexers are healthy with [Check server health and topology](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/server.md).

## Review fired alerts

Source: https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/alerts.md


When to use: an incident is under way and you need to see which rules fired, when, and at what severity; a maintenance window is coming and noisy rules must be throttled before they flood the on-call channel; or an auditor asks which alerts fired and which were suppressed.

### Prerequisites

- A profile that passes `splunkctl doctor` (see [Configure](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/configure.md)).
- Read access to fired alerts for `list`, `get`, and `actions`.
- Write access to the saved search that owns the rule for `suppress` and `unsuppress`.

### Synopsis

```text
splunkctl alerts list [--filter SUBSTRING] [--limit N] [--offset N]
splunkctl alerts get <NAME>
splunkctl alerts actions
splunkctl alerts suppress <NAME> [--duration SECONDS] [--yes]
splunkctl alerts unsuppress <NAME> [--yes]
```

`NAME` is the rule's saved search name, matched exactly and case-sensitively.

### Workflow

#### Triage during an incident

```bash
splunkctl alerts list
splunkctl alerts list --filter brute
splunkctl alerts get 'Brute Force Login Attempts'
```

Expected result: one row per firing with `rule`, `triggered`, `severity`, `sid`, and `actions`. `--filter` matches the rule name; `--limit` and `--offset` page the firing rows client side, so a row is one firing, not one rule. `get` prints every firing of one rule and the firing count.

#### Check alert action types

```bash
splunkctl alerts actions
```

Expected result: the action types (email, webhook, script, and app-provided actions) configured on the instance. Check this before creating or changing saved searches that fire alerts.

#### Suppress during a maintenance window

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host in the active profile. Impact: `alert.suppress=1` and `alert.suppress.period=<SECONDS>s` are written to the rule's saved search, so repeat firings are throttled for that window. Preview with `splunkctl alerts suppress 'Brute Force Login Attempts' --duration 7200`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl conf get savedsearches 'Brute Force Login Attempts' --key alert.suppress`.

```bash
splunkctl alerts suppress 'Brute Force Login Attempts' --duration 7200
splunkctl alerts suppress 'Brute Force Login Attempts' --duration 7200 --yes
```

Expected result: the preview prints `[DRY RUN] Throttle alerts for rule (profile: NAME @ HOST:8089)` and the settings it will write; the apply prints `Throttled 'Brute Force Login Attempts' for 7200s.`. `--duration` is in seconds and defaults to 3600. Splunk's fired-alerts endpoint cannot be edited; throttling is a property of the underlying saved search.

Suppress several rules during a planned outage:

```bash
for rule in 'Brute Force Login Attempts' 'Failed VPN Auth' 'DNS Exfil'; do
  splunkctl alerts suppress "$rule" --duration 14400 --yes
done
```

#### Remove suppression after the window

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host in the active profile. Impact: `alert.suppress=0` is written to the rule's saved search and it alerts normally again. Preview with `splunkctl alerts unsuppress 'Brute Force Login Attempts'`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl conf get savedsearches 'Brute Force Login Attempts' --key alert.suppress`.

```bash
splunkctl alerts unsuppress 'Brute Force Login Attempts'
splunkctl alerts unsuppress 'Brute Force Login Attempts' --yes
```

Expected result: `Removed throttling from 'Brute Force Login Attempts'.`. The throttle setting stays on the saved search until you remove it; it does not expire on its own.

#### Produce JSON for scripts and agents

```bash
splunkctl alerts list --json
splunkctl alerts list --json | jq '.[] | select((.severity | tonumber) >= 5)'
splunkctl alerts get 'Brute Force Login Attempts' --json > alert_detail.json
```

Expected result: a JSON array of firing rows, suitable for `jq`, an agent, or audit evidence. `--format table|json|csv|jsonl` picks another output format. An agent can consume the JSON directly to correlate fired alerts with a change calendar or file tickets for high-severity triggers.

### Troubleshooting

- `not_found` from `alerts get`: the name must match the rule exactly; run `splunkctl alerts list --filter <text>` to find the spelling.
- `not_found` from `suppress` or `unsuppress`: no saved search with that name is visible to your account; check `splunkctl rules list --filter <text>`.
- `permission` from `suppress` or `unsuppress`: your role cannot edit the saved search in its owning app.
- `No fired alerts.`: nothing has fired within Splunk's fired-alert retention; this is not an error.
- A rule keeps firing after `suppress --yes`: throttling suppresses repeat firings for the period after a trigger; it does not disable the search. Disable the rule itself with the commands in [Manage detection rules](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/rules.md).

### See also

- [Manage detection rules](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/rules.md)
- [Triage ES notables](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/es.md)
- [Edit any conf file](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/conf.md)
- [Command reference: alerts](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/commands/alerts.md)

## Triage ES notables

Source: https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/es.md


When to use: you work the Enterprise Security incident review queue and want to see what is open, pull the full detail of one notable, then assign it, change its status or urgency, set a disposition, or leave a comment, alone or in bulk.

### Prerequisites

- Splunk Enterprise Security installed on the target instance. Every `es` subcommand first checks for the `SplunkEnterpriseSecuritySuite` app and exits 1 with a `not_found` error when it is missing.
- A Splunk account that can search `index=notable` and call the `notable_update` endpoint (the ES analyst role or equivalent).
- Live verification against a real ES instance is still pending for this group. The read and update logic is unit-tested against a mocked REST layer; the feature-detection path is the only part verified live. Test on a non-production ES instance before scripting production triage.

### Synopsis

```text
splunkctl es notables list [--since TIME] [--until TIME] [--status NAME_OR_INT] [--owner USER] [--rule SUBSTRING] [--limit N]
splunkctl es notables get <EVENT_ID>
splunkctl es notables update <EVENT_IDS>... [--status NAME_OR_INT] [--owner USER] [--urgency informational|low|medium|high|critical] [--disposition ID] [--comment TEXT] [--yes]
```

### Workflow

#### See the queue

```bash
splunkctl es notables list
splunkctl es notables list --since -7d --status new
splunkctl es notables list --owner unassigned
splunkctl es notables list --rule beacon --limit 20
splunkctl es notables list --json
```

The default window is the last 24 hours, up to 100 rows. `--since` and `--until` become the search time range; `--status`, `--owner`, and `--rule` fold into the SPL (`index=notable status=1 owner="analyst1" rule_name="*beacon*"`) so filtering happens server side. Expected columns: `time`, `rule`, `security_domain`, `urgency`, `status`, `owner`, `event_id`. Pass `event_id` straight to `get` or `update`.

#### Read one notable

```bash
splunkctl es notables get <EVENT_ID>
splunkctl es notables get <EVENT_ID> --json
```

Returns the full field set of the notable event.

#### Triage one or many notables

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host in the active profile. Impact: status, owner, urgency, disposition, or comment changes on every event id you pass, in one `notable_update` call. Preview with `splunkctl es notables update <EVENT_ID> --status closed --comment 'false positive'`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl es notables get <EVENT_ID>`.

```bash
splunkctl es notables update <EVENT_ID> --status closed \
  --comment 'false positive, ticket CHG-123'
splunkctl es notables update <EVENT_ID> --status closed \
  --comment 'false positive, ticket CHG-123' --yes
splunkctl es notables update <ID1> <ID2> <ID3> --owner analyst1 --urgency high --yes
splunkctl es notables update <ID1> <ID2> --status closed --comment 'duplicate of INC-4471' --yes
```

The preview looks like this:

```text
$ splunkctl es notables update evt-1 evt-2 --status closed --comment 'fp'
[DRY RUN] Update 2 notable(s) (profile: default @ splunk.example.com:8089)
  event_ids: evt-1, evt-2
  changes: status=5, comment=fp
Pass --yes to apply.
```

At least one of `--status`, `--owner`, `--urgency`, `--disposition`, or `--comment` is required; `update` with no change is a usage error (exit 2). The preview is local only; the ES feature check runs when `--yes` is passed.

#### Status names and integers

`--status` on `list` and `update` accepts the name or the integer ES stores:

| Name | Integer |
|---|---|
| `unassigned` | 0 |
| `new` | 1 |
| `in progress` | 2 |
| `pending` | 3 |
| `resolved` | 4 |
| `closed` | 5 |

Custom statuses from `reviewstatuses.conf` are integers above 5; pass the number, for example `--status 6`.

#### Dispositions

`--disposition` is passed through as given. ES ships `disposition:1` (true positive), `disposition:2` (benign positive), `disposition:3` (false positive), and more, but installations customize the list, so check your instance's Incident Review disposition dropdown or `reviewstatuses.conf` before scripting against an id.

### Troubleshooting

- `{"error": {"kind": "not_found", ...}}` naming `SplunkEnterpriseSecuritySuite`: ES is not installed on this instance, or the account cannot see the app.
- Exit 2 on `update`: no change flag was given.
- `list` returns nothing: widen `--since` (for example `--since -7d`) or drop `--status`.
- A custom status name is rejected: use its integer.

### See also

- [Manage ES correlations and threat intel](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/es-detections.md)
- [Run searches](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/search.md)
- [Review fired alerts](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/alerts.md)
- [Ingest SIEM results into SOAR](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/soar-ingest.md)
- [Command reference: es](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/commands/es.md)

## Manage dashboards

Source: https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/dashboards.md


When to use: you want dashboard XML or Studio JSON in version control, need to copy a dashboard between instances, or must change who can see one.

### Prerequisites

- A Splunk account with write access to the target app (for example the `admin` or `power` role in `search`).

### Synopsis

```text
splunkctl dashboards list [--app APP] [--all] [--filter SUBSTRING] [--limit N] [--offset N]
splunkctl dashboards get <NAME> [--app APP] [--definition]
splunkctl dashboards export [NAME] [--app APP] [--out FILE] [--definition] [--all --dir DIR]
splunkctl dashboards create --name <NAME> --file <FILE> [--app APP] [--type classic|studio|auto] [--sharing user|app|global] [--yes]
splunkctl dashboards update <NAME> --file <FILE> [--app APP] [--type classic|studio|auto] [--yes]
splunkctl dashboards share <NAME> --sharing <user|app|global> [--owner USER] [--app APP] [--yes]
splunkctl dashboards delete <NAME> [--app APP] [--yes]
```

`--app` defaults to `search` for the mutation commands.

### Workflow

#### List and inspect

```bash
splunkctl dashboards list
splunkctl dashboards list --app search --filter soc
splunkctl dashboards get soc_overview --app search
splunkctl dashboards get soc_studio --definition
```

`list` shows dashboards only; add `--all` to include other views. `--filter`, `--limit`, and `--offset` apply client side after the app and type filters. `get` prints the XML source; `--definition` extracts the Studio JSON and errors on a Classic dashboard.

#### Export to files

```bash
splunkctl dashboards export soc_overview --out dashboards/soc_overview.xml
splunkctl dashboards export soc_studio --definition --out dashboards/soc_studio.json
splunkctl dashboards export --all --dir dashboards/
```

Expected result: one file per dashboard, ready to commit. `--out` overwrites without prompting.

#### Create a dashboard from a file

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host and app in the active profile (`--app`, default `search`). Impact: a new dashboard appears in that app. Preview with `splunkctl dashboards create --name new_dash --file dash.xml --app search`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl dashboards get new_dash --app search`.

```bash
splunkctl dashboards create --name new_dash --file dash.xml --app search
splunkctl dashboards create --name new_dash --file dash.xml --app search --yes
splunkctl dashboards create --name new_dash --file dash.json --type studio --sharing app --yes
```

`--type auto` (the default) detects Classic XML or Studio JSON from the file.

#### Update a dashboard

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host and app in the active profile. Impact: the dashboard source is replaced with the file's content. Preview with `splunkctl dashboards update soc_overview --file updated.xml`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl dashboards get soc_overview`.

```bash
splunkctl dashboards update soc_overview --file updated.xml --app search
splunkctl dashboards update soc_overview --file updated.xml --app search --yes
```

Export first so you can restore the previous version if needed.

#### Change sharing

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host and app in the active profile. Impact: who can see the dashboard changes; `global` makes it visible from every app. Preview with `splunkctl dashboards share soc_overview --sharing app`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl dashboards list --filter soc_overview --json` (check `sharing`).

```bash
splunkctl dashboards share soc_overview --sharing app --yes
splunkctl dashboards share soc_overview --sharing global --owner admin --yes
```

#### Delete a dashboard

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host and app in the active profile. Impact: the dashboard is removed and cannot be recovered except from an export. Preview with `splunkctl dashboards delete old_dash --app search`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl dashboards list --app search --filter old_dash`.

```bash
splunkctl dashboards export old_dash --out backup/old_dash.xml
splunkctl dashboards delete old_dash --app search
splunkctl dashboards delete old_dash --app search --yes
```

### Troubleshooting

- `not_found` on `get` or `update`: pass `--app`; the dashboard may live outside `search`.
- `--definition` errors: the dashboard is Classic XML, not Studio.
- `permission` on create or share: the account lacks write access to the app, or `global` sharing needs the `admin_all_objects` capability.

### See also

- [Manage configuration as code](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/state.md), which pulls and diffs dashboards
- [Run searches](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/search.md)
- [Install](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/install.md)
- [Command reference: dashboards](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/commands/dashboards.md)

## Manage detection rules

Source: https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/rules.md


When to use: you maintain scheduled saved searches (detections) and want to create or tune them from the terminal, keep them in git, review changes in a pull request, and promote them from staging to production with a preview of every change.

### Prerequisites

- A Splunk account that can create and schedule saved searches in the target app (for example the `power` or `admin` role).
- For `--actions notable` or `risk`, Enterprise Security installed on the target.
- For `import`: a YAML file produced by `rules export` or written in the shape shown under "Export to YAML".

### Synopsis

```text
splunkctl rules list [--app APP] [--owner USER] [--scheduled] [--filter SUBSTRING] [--limit N] [--offset N]
splunkctl rules get <NAME> [--app APP] [--owner USER]
splunkctl rules history <NAME>
splunkctl rules schedule [--app APP] [--owner USER] [--filter SUBSTRING] [--limit N] [--offset N]
splunkctl rules test <NAME> [--earliest TIME] [--latest TIME] [--limit N]
splunkctl rules create --name <NAME> --search <SPL> [--cron EXPR] [--app APP] [--description TEXT] [--actions LIST] [--disabled] [--earliest TIME] [--latest TIME] [--alert-type TYPE] [--alert-comparator CMP] [--alert-threshold N] [--severity 1-6] [--throttle SECONDS] [--throttle-fields LIST] [--track|--no-track] [--schedule-window N|auto] [--email-to LIST] [--email-subject TEXT] [--webhook-url URL] [--set KEY=VALUE]... [--yes]
splunkctl rules update <NAME> [same flags as create except --name, plus --enabled|--disabled] [--yes]
splunkctl rules enable <NAME> [--yes]
splunkctl rules disable <NAME> [--yes]
splunkctl rules share <NAME> --sharing <user|app|global> [--owner USER] [--yes]
splunkctl rules delete <NAME> [--yes]
splunkctl rules export --path <FILE.yml> [--name NAME]... [--app APP]
splunkctl rules import --path <FILE.yml> [--update|--no-update] [--yes]
```

### Workflow

#### List and inspect rules

```bash
splunkctl rules list
splunkctl rules list --scheduled
splunkctl rules get 'Brute Force - Multiple Failed Logins'
splunkctl rules history 'Brute Force - Multiple Failed Logins'
splunkctl rules list --json | jq '.[] | select(.is_scheduled == "0")'
```

Expected result: one row per saved search; `get` adds the SPL and every saved-search field; `history` lists past runs. `--json` gives structured output for scripts and agents.

`list` and `get` default to the current namespace, which does not include saved searches private to a specific app (for example rules shipped by an add-on such as Splunk_Security_Essentials). Pass `--app` to scope into that namespace; the owner is wildcarded automatically, so app-private rules owned by any user are included. Add `--owner` only to narrow to one user's rules:

```bash
splunkctl rules list --app Splunk_Security_Essentials
splunkctl rules get 'Generate MITRE Detections Lookup' --app Splunk_Security_Essentials
```

#### Check scheduler health

```bash
splunkctl rules schedule
splunkctl rules schedule --json
splunkctl rules schedule --app search
```

Expected result: a table with `name`, `cron`, `next_run`, `window`, and `enabled` for every scheduled saved search. JSON output adds `cron_schedule`, `next_scheduled_time`, `dispatch.earliest_time`, `dispatch.latest_time`, `is_scheduled`, `disabled`, and `qualifiedSearch`.

#### Create a rule

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host and app in the active profile. Impact: a new scheduled search that starts running on its cron and fires its alert actions. Preview with `splunkctl rules create --name 'Lateral Movement - PsExec' --search 'index=win EventCode=7045 ServiceName="PSEXESVC"' --cron '*/5 * * * *' --actions notable`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl rules get 'Lateral Movement - PsExec'`.

```bash
splunkctl rules create --name 'Lateral Movement - PsExec' \
    --search 'index=win EventCode=7045 ServiceName="PSEXESVC"' \
    --cron '*/5 * * * *' --actions notable --yes
splunkctl rules create --name 'Rule' --search '<SPL>' \
    --cron '*/5 * * * *' --actions email --email-to soc@bank.example --yes
splunkctl rules create --name 'Rule' --search '<SPL>' --cron '*/5 * * * *' \
    --alert-comparator 'greater than' --alert-threshold 10 --severity 4 \
    --throttle 3600 --throttle-fields src --disabled --yes
```

Expected result: the rule exists; with `--disabled` it is created but not scheduled until you `enable` it.

`--email-to`, `--email-subject`, and `--webhook-url` are shortcuts for the most common alert-action fields, on both `create` and `update`:

| Flag | Field | Requires |
|---|---|---|
| `--email-to` | `action.email.to` | `--actions email` to enable |
| `--email-subject` | `action.email.subject` | `--actions email` to enable |
| `--webhook-url` | `action.webhook.param.url` | `--actions webhook` to enable |

Setting a flag does not enable its action; Splunk keeps `action.*` params inert until the action is named in `--actions`. Passing a flag whose action is not enabled prints a non-blocking advisory (`--email-to is set but 'email' is not in --actions`) and still applies. On `update` the advisory is based on the current invocation's `--actions`, so it can fire even when the action is already enabled server-side (for example when rotating an email recipient without repeating `--actions email`). A flag and an equivalent `--set` for the same field is a usage error (exit 2), not a silent pick:

```bash
splunkctl rules create --name 'Rule' --search '<SPL>' \
    --email-to soc@bank.example --set action.email.to=other@bank.example
```

`--set action.*` is the escape hatch for any action field without a flag (ES notable and risk params, `action.webhook.param.method`, and so on).

#### Update, enable, or disable a rule

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host and app in the active profile. Impact: the SPL, schedule, or actions change for the next run; `disable` stops the detection from firing. Preview with `splunkctl rules update 'Rule' --search '<SPL>'`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl rules get 'Rule'`.

```bash
splunkctl rules update 'Rule' --search '<SPL>' --yes
splunkctl rules update 'Rule' --cron '*/10 * * * *' --earliest -15m --latest now --yes
splunkctl rules enable 'Rule' --yes
splunkctl rules disable 'Rule' --yes
```

Expected result: `get` shows the new field values; `enable` and `disable` flip `disabled`.

#### Test a rule without firing actions

```bash
splunkctl rules test 'Rule'
splunkctl rules test 'Rule' --earliest -7d --latest now --limit 500
```

Expected result: the saved search is dispatched now over its window (or the override) and the results print, without triggering alert actions. Use it to backfill or to tune a threshold before enabling.

#### Change sharing

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host and app in the active profile. Impact: who can see and run the rule changes; `global` exposes it from every app. Preview with `splunkctl rules share 'Rule' --sharing app`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl rules get 'Rule' --json` (check the ACL).

```bash
splunkctl rules share 'Rule' --sharing app --yes
splunkctl rules share 'Rule' --sharing global --owner admin --yes
```

#### Delete a rule

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host and app in the active profile. Impact: the saved search is removed and its detection stops; only an export can restore it. Preview with `splunkctl rules delete 'Rule'`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl rules list --filter 'Rule'`.

```bash
splunkctl rules export --path backup.yml --name 'Rule'
splunkctl rules delete 'Rule' --yes
```

#### Export to YAML

```bash
splunkctl rules export --path detections.yml
splunkctl rules export --path ess.yml --app SplunkEnterpriseSecuritySuite
splunkctl rules export --path brute.yml --name 'Brute Force' --name 'Credential Stuffing'
```

Expected result: a YAML list, one document per rule. `--name` is repeatable; `--app` filters by app context. The file looks like this:

```yaml
- name: "Brute Force - Multiple Failed Logins"
  search: >
    index=auth sourcetype=linux_secure action=failure
    | bin _time span=5m
    | stats count dc(user) as users values(user) as targets by src
    | where count > 20 AND users > 3
  description: "Distributed brute force across multiple accounts"
  cron_schedule: "*/10 * * * *"
  is_scheduled: "1"
  actions: "email,notable"
  alert.severity: "4"
  alert.suppress: "1"
  alert.suppress.period: "1h"
  alert.suppress.fields: "src"
  dispatch.earliest_time: "-15m"
  dispatch.latest_time: "now"
```

| Field | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | yes | Saved search name (unique per app) |
| `search` | yes | SPL query |
| `description` | no | Human-readable summary |
| `cron_schedule` | no | Cron expression (auto-sets `is_scheduled`) |
| `is_scheduled` | no | `"1"` to enable scheduling |
| `disabled` | no | `"1"` to create in disabled state |
| `actions` | no | Alert actions, comma-separated (`email`, `notable`) |
| `alert_type` | no | Trigger condition type |
| `alert.severity` | no | `"1"` (info) through `"6"` (critical) |
| `alert.suppress` | no | `"1"` to suppress; set `.period` and `.fields` |
| `alert.track` | no | `"1"` to track triggered alert count |
| `dispatch.earliest_time` | no | Search window start (for example `"-1h"`) |
| `dispatch.latest_time` | no | Search window end (for example `"now"`) |
| `app` | no | App context (omitted defaults to `search`) |

Any `SavedSearch` REST API attribute can be included; unknown keys pass through as-is.

#### Import with a preview

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host in the active profile (set `SPLUNK_HOST` or `--profile` to pick staging or prod). Impact: rules in the file are created or updated; nothing is deleted. Preview with `splunkctl rules import --path detections.yml` and read the per-rule create, update, or unchanged lines with field-level diffs, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl rules get <NAME>`.

```bash
splunkctl rules import --path detections.yml
splunkctl rules import --path detections.yml --json
splunkctl rules import --path detections.yml --yes
splunkctl rules import --path detections.yml --no-update --yes
SPLUNK_HOST=prod.corp splunkctl rules import --path detections.yml --yes
```

Expected result: the dry run prints one line per rule on stderr; with `--json` it also prints a full diff array on stdout, one object per rule: `{"name", "action", "changes": [{"field", "old", "new"}], "reason"}` where `action` is `create`, `update`, `unchanged`, or `skip`. The command exits non-zero when any rule is skipped or fails. `--no-update` seeds a fresh instance without clobbering rules analysts have tuned in place.

#### Run the detection-as-code loop

> **Safety:** Target is whichever Splunk host `SPLUNK_HOST` or `--profile` selects for each step. Impact: the staging and then the prod instance receive every rule in the file. Preview with `splunkctl rules import --path detections.yml`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl rules list --scheduled` on the target.

```bash
splunkctl rules export --path detections.yml
git add detections.yml && git commit -m "Tune brute force threshold"
splunkctl rules import --path detections.yml
splunkctl rules import --path detections.yml --yes
SPLUNK_HOST=prod.corp splunkctl rules import --path detections.yml --yes
```

Expected result: every SPL change is a commit with author and diff, goes through pull-request review, is linted in CI, is previewed on staging, and is promoted to prod from the same file. [Manage configuration as code](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/state.md) wraps this loop with a change-ticket report.

### Troubleshooting

- `not_found` on `get` or `update`: the rule is app-private; pass `--app <APP>`.
- Usage error (exit 2) on `create` or `update`: you passed both `--email-to` (or `--email-subject`, `--webhook-url`) and the equivalent `--set` field. Keep one.
- `permission` on `create`, `share`, or `import`: the account cannot write saved searches in the app, or `--sharing global` needs the `admin_all_objects` capability.
- `http` error mentioning cron: Splunk rejected `--cron`; use five fields (`*/5 * * * *`).
- `import` exits 1 after applying some rules: at least one rule was skipped; its `reason` is in the `--json` output. Rerun after fixing, the rest is idempotent.
- The email action never sends: `--email-to` alone does not enable it; add `--actions email`.

### See also

- [Manage configuration as code](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/state.md)
- [Review fired alerts](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/alerts.md)
- [Manage ES correlations and threat intel](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/es-detections.md)
- [Run searches](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/search.md)
- [Command reference: rules](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/commands/rules.md)

## Manage ES correlations and threat intel

Source: https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/es-detections.md


When to use: you maintain the detections that generate Enterprise Security notables and the threat-intelligence collections they match against, and you want to enable, disable, or inspect them without opening Splunk Web.

### Prerequisites

- Splunk Enterprise Security installed on the target instance. Every `es` subcommand checks for the `SplunkEnterpriseSecuritySuite` app and exits 1 with a `not_found` error when it is missing.
- A Splunk account that can read and edit saved searches in the `SplunkEnterpriseSecuritySuite` app and call the `/services/data/threat_intel/*` endpoints.
- Live verification against a real ES instance is still pending for this group; the logic is unit-tested against a mocked REST layer. Test on a non-production ES instance first.

### Synopsis

```text
splunkctl es correlations list [--enabled | --disabled] [--security-domain NAME]
splunkctl es correlations get <NAME>
splunkctl es correlations enable <NAMES>... [--yes]
splunkctl es correlations disable <NAMES>... [--yes]
splunkctl es threat-intel list [--type COLLECTION] [--limit N]
splunkctl es threat-intel upload --type <COLLECTION> --file <FILE> [--yes]
splunkctl es threat-intel delete <KEY> [--yes]
```

Collection types: `ip_intel`, `domain_intel`, `file_intel`, `email_intel`, `http_intel`, `certificate_intel`, `registry_intel`, `service_intel`, `user_intel`, `process_intel`.

### Workflow

#### Review correlation searches

```bash
splunkctl es correlations list
splunkctl es correlations list --enabled
splunkctl es correlations list --disabled
splunkctl es correlations list --security-domain access
splunkctl es correlations get "Brute Force Access Behavior"
```

Correlation searches are saved searches scoped to the `SplunkEnterpriseSecuritySuite` app; the CLI fetches across all owners. `list` shows `name`, `security_domain`, `severity`, `enabled`, `cron_schedule`, and `next_scheduled_time`. `get` adds `search`, `description`, `is_scheduled`, `actions`, `dispatch.earliest_time`, `dispatch.latest_time`, `app`, `owner`, and `sharing`. The security domain is read from `action.correlationsearch.label`, falling back to `security_domain`.

#### Enable or disable correlation searches

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host in the active profile. Impact: the named searches start or stop generating notables on their next schedule. Preview with `splunkctl es correlations disable "DNS Exfil"`, apply with `splunkctl es correlations disable "DNS Exfil" --yes`, and verify with `splunkctl es correlations get "DNS Exfil"` (check `enabled`).

```bash
splunkctl es correlations enable "Brute Force Access Behavior"
splunkctl es correlations enable "Rule A" "Rule B" --yes
splunkctl es correlations disable "DNS Exfil" --yes
```

#### List threat-intelligence items

```bash
splunkctl es threat-intel list
splunkctl es threat-intel list --type ip_intel
splunkctl es threat-intel list --type domain_intel --limit 25
```

Reads `/services/data/threat_intel/item`, up to 100 rows by default. The `name` column is the key you pass to `delete`.

#### Upload indicators

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host in the active profile. Impact: every row in the file becomes a threat-intel item in the chosen collection and can match against live events. Preview with `splunkctl es threat-intel upload --type ip_intel --file iocs.csv`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl es threat-intel list --type ip_intel`.

```bash
splunkctl es threat-intel upload --type ip_intel --file iocs.csv
splunkctl es threat-intel upload --type ip_intel --file iocs.csv --yes
```

`--file` takes a local CSV or JSON file. A CSV needs a header row that matches the fields of the collection type, for example `ip`, `description`, and `weight` for `ip_intel`:

```csv
ip,description,weight
203.0.113.10,known C2,80
```

#### Delete an indicator

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host in the active profile. Impact: the item stops matching. Preview with `splunkctl es threat-intel delete <KEY>`, apply with `splunkctl es threat-intel delete <KEY> --yes`, and verify with `splunkctl es threat-intel list --type <COLLECTION>`.

```bash
splunkctl es threat-intel delete <KEY> --yes
```

`KEY` is the `name` value from `threat-intel list`.

### Troubleshooting

- `{"error": {"kind": "not_found", ...}}` naming `SplunkEnterpriseSecuritySuite`: ES is not installed or not visible to this account.
- A correlation search is not listed: it may be owned by another app; `es correlations` only covers the ES app. Use `splunkctl rules list` for other saved searches.
- Upload is accepted but items do not appear: check that the CSV header matches the collection's field names.

### See also

- [Triage ES notables](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/es.md)
- [Manage detection rules](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/rules.md)
- [Manage lookups](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/lookups.md)
- [Command reference: es](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/commands/es.md)

## Manage macros, eventtypes, tags

Source: https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/knowledge.md


When to use: a detection depends on a macro, an eventtype, or a CIM tag and you need to read or change it without remembering the stanza-naming rules of `macros.conf`, `eventtypes.conf`, and `tags.conf`. Only `macros set` mutates; `eventtypes` and `tags` are read-only.

### Prerequisites

- A profile that passes `splunkctl doctor` (see [Configure](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/configure.md)).
- Write access to the app that owns `macros.conf` for `macros set`.
- For anything these verbs do not cover (creating or editing an eventtype or a tag assignment, or any other conf file), use [Edit any conf file](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/conf.md); these commands share `conf`'s stanza core rather than re-implementing it.

### Synopsis

```text
splunkctl macros list [--app APP] [--filter SUBSTRING] [--limit N] [--offset N]
splunkctl macros get <NAME> [--app APP]
splunkctl macros set <NAME> --definition <SPL> [--args A,B] [--yes]
splunkctl eventtypes list [--app APP] [--filter SUBSTRING] [--limit N] [--offset N]
splunkctl eventtypes get <NAME> [--app APP]
splunkctl tags list [--app APP] [--filter SUBSTRING] [--limit N] [--offset N]
splunkctl tags get <FIELD=VALUE> [--app APP]
```

Two stanza shapes make these verbs worth having over raw `conf`: a macro with arguments is stored as `name(argcount)`, not `name`, and a `tags.conf` stanza is a `field=value` pair whose keys are tag names rather than config keys.

### Workflow

#### Read macros

```bash
splunkctl macros list --app Splunk_Security_Essentials
splunkctl macros list --filter Sort
splunkctl macros get Sort_MITRE_Rows
splunkctl macros get "Sort_MITRE_Rows(1)"
```

Expected result: `list` shows each macro with its definition; `get` prints the full stanza. Splunk stores a macro that takes arguments under `name(n)` where `n` is the argument count (`Sort_MITRE_Rows(1)`, not `Sort_MITRE_Rows`). `macros get <name>` tries an exact stanza match first, which covers a no-arg macro or a name spelled out with its `(n)` suffix; if that misses and the name has no `(...)` of its own, it falls back to the `macros.conf` listing and picks the argument-form stanza whose base name matches. If more than one arg-count variant of the same base name exists (unusual, but legal), the lowest arg count wins; pass the full `name(n)` to reach the others.

#### Audit what a detection's macro expands to

```bash
splunkctl rules get my_detection --json | jq -r .search
splunkctl macros get my_detection_macro --json | jq -r .definition
```

Expected result: the rule's SPL and the macro definition it calls. Long `definition` and `search` values are truncated for table display only (`... [+N chars]`); `--json` and `--format json` always carry the full text.

#### Create or update a macro

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host in the active profile and `macros.conf` in the current app namespace. Impact: the stanza `NAME` (or `NAME(n)` with `--args`) is created or its `definition` replaced, and every search that calls the macro changes behaviour immediately. Preview with `splunkctl macros set my_macro --definition 'index=main'`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl macros get my_macro`.

```bash
splunkctl macros set my_macro --definition 'index=main'
splunkctl macros set my_macro --definition 'index=main' --yes
splunkctl macros set my_macro --definition 'eval x=$a$+$b$' --args a,b --yes
```

Expected result: the preview shows a field-level diff (`definition: add -> ...` for a new macro, `old -> new` for an update), the same mechanism as `conf set`; the apply prints `Created macro 'my_macro' (1 key(s)).` or `Updated ...`. The third example writes the stanza `my_macro(2)`.

`macros set` does no argument-form resolution: it is a thin name-to-stanza mapping, not a lookup. `--args a,b` computes `name(2)`, no `--args` computes the bare `name`, and that is the stanza written whether or not it existed. To update an existing arg-form macro, pass `--args` with the same argument count, or use `splunkctl conf set macros "name(n)" definition=... --yes` directly, which is also the way to change a macro's arg count.

#### Read eventtypes

```bash
splunkctl eventtypes list
splunkctl eventtypes list --app Splunk_SA_CIM --filter cim: --json | jq '[.[] | {name, search}]'
splunkctl eventtypes get cim:authentication
```

Expected result: `list` shows `name`, `search`, `app`, and `disabled`; `get` prints the full stanza (search, tags, priority, color). The second example finds every eventtype backing a CIM data model.

#### Check whether an eventtype is tagged

```bash
splunkctl tags list
splunkctl tags get "eventtype=cim:authentication"
splunkctl tags get "eventtype=cim%3Aauthentication"
```

Expected result: `tags list` shows one row per `field=value` stanza with only the enabled tag names (`;`-joined), a quick "what does this event carry" summary; `tags get` shows every tag key and its actual state, enabled or disabled, for full-detail auditing. Every key inside a `tags.conf` stanza is a tag name whose value is `enabled` or `disabled`; the top-level `disabled` key is the stanza's own flag, not a tag, and is excluded from both views. Splunk's REST layer percent-encodes a colon inside a tag value (`cim:authentication` becomes `cim%3Aauthentication`); `tags list` prints the decoded name, and `tags get` accepts either form.

### Troubleshooting

- `not_found` from `macros get`, `eventtypes get`, or `tags get`: the object lives in another app; pass `--app APP`. The unscoped default namespace can miss app-private stanzas, the same as `conf list` and `rules list`, and `get` uses `--app` to disambiguate a name that exists in more than one app.
- `macros set --yes` created a second stanza instead of updating: the existing macro is arg-form (`name(n)`) and you omitted `--args`, or passed a different count; rerun with the matching `--args`, then clear the stray stanza with `splunkctl conf unset macros NAME definition --yes`.
- `permission` from `macros set`: the account cannot write `macros.conf` in that app.
- `tags get` reports `Stanza 'X' not found in tags.conf`: copy the `field_value` exactly as `tags list` prints it, including the `field=` prefix.
- A macro change has no effect in searches: macros are read at search time, so the next search picks it up; check the definition with `macros get` and the calling rule with `rules get`.

### See also

- [Edit any conf file](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/conf.md)
- [Manage detection rules](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/rules.md)
- [Check data model acceleration](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/datamodels.md)
- [Manage configuration as code](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/state.md)
- [Command reference: macros](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/commands/macros.md), [eventtypes](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/commands/eventtypes.md), [tags](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/commands/tags.md)

## Check data model acceleration

Source: https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/datamodels.md


When to use: your detections run on accelerated CIM data models through `| tstats` and you need to know which models exist, whether acceleration is healthy and complete, and how to trigger a rebuild when a summary is stale or broken.

### Prerequisites

- A profile that passes `splunkctl doctor` (see [Configure](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/configure.md)).
- Read access to data models for `list`, `get`, and `acceleration`; write access to the model's app (for example `Splunk_SA_CIM`) for `rebuild`.
- Every command is a thin, typed wrapper around the `datamodel/model` and `admin/summarization` REST collections.

### Synopsis

```text
splunkctl datamodels list [--app APP] [--filter SUBSTRING] [--limit N] [--offset N]
splunkctl datamodels get <NAME> [--app APP] [--definition]
splunkctl datamodels acceleration [NAME]
splunkctl datamodels rebuild <NAME> [--app APP] [--yes]
```

### Workflow

#### List the models

```bash
splunkctl datamodels list
splunkctl datamodels list --app Splunk_SA_CIM
splunkctl datamodels list --filter auth
```

Expected result: `name`, `app`, `accelerated` (bool), and `disabled` (bool), read straight off the collection listing with no per-model follow-up call. `--app` defaults to all apps. `--filter` forces a full fetch with client-side case-insensitive name matching; without it, `--limit` and `--offset` pass straight through to the REST call as `count` and `offset`.

#### Inspect one model

```bash
splunkctl datamodels get Authentication
splunkctl datamodels get Authentication --app Splunk_SA_CIM
splunkctl datamodels get Authentication --definition
```

Expected result: a detection-engineering summary rather than the full blob. A model's raw definition is a JSON-encoded string that can run past 250 KB for a CIM model with dozens of objects; `get` parses it once and surfaces:

- `name`, `app`, `displayName`, `disabled`
- `acceleration_enabled`, `acceleration_earliest_time`, `acceleration_cron_schedule`: the acceleration configuration, not build status
- `object_count`, `objects` (comma-joined object names)
- `root_search`: the base object's first constraint search, which is the raw index, sourcetype, or tag the whole model covers

`--definition` prints the raw, pretty-printed objects, fields, and calculations JSON instead, the same shape as `dashboards get --definition` but for a model's object hierarchy.

#### Check acceleration health

```bash
splunkctl datamodels acceleration
splunkctl datamodels acceleration Authentication
```

Expected result: without a name, one row per model whose acceleration configuration is enabled; with a name, that model whether or not it is accelerated. Each row carries:

- `enabled`: acceleration configuration state
- `has_summary`: whether `admin/summarization` has an entity yet; a freshly enabled model whose cron has not fired is `enabled: true, has_summary: false`, accelerated but nothing built
- `is_complete` and `percent_complete`: from `summary.complete`, a 0 to 1 fraction server side, rendered as a 0 to 100 percentage rounded to one decimal place
- `size`, `earliest_summarized`, `latest_summarized`: raw `summary.size`, `summary.earliest_time`, and `summary.latest_time`, unmodified (epoch seconds)
- `last_error`: `summary.last_error` (a list server side, one entry per distributed peer) joined with `; `; empty when clean

Two REST resources are involved because `datamodel/model`'s `acceleration` field holds only the configuration (`enabled`, `earliest_time`, `cron_schedule`) and never build progress. Percent complete, the summarized range, size, and the last build error live on a separate `admin/summarization` entity per accelerated model, named `tstats:DM_<app>_<model>`, the same source Splunk Web's Data Model Manager page reads. If nothing is accelerated, the command renders an empty result, never an error, and skips the `admin/summarization` fetch. `acceleration <name>` on a non-accelerated model returns `enabled: false` with the other fields blank or `null`; that is a valid answer to "is this model accelerated at all", so an agent auditing coverage does not need a special case. Only a model that does not exist is an error (`not_found`).

#### Rebuild a stale summary

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host in the active profile and the named model's app. Impact: the existing tsidx summary is dropped and historical data is re-summarized from scratch for the same `earliest_time` window; `| tstats` searches run on incomplete data until the rebuild finishes. Preview with `splunkctl datamodels rebuild Authentication`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl datamodels acceleration Authentication` until `percent_complete` reaches 100.

```bash
splunkctl datamodels rebuild Authentication
splunkctl datamodels rebuild Authentication --yes
splunkctl datamodels acceleration Authentication
```

Expected result: the preview names the model, its app, the preserved `earliest_time` window, and states that this re-summarizes historical data from scratch; there is no partial or incremental rebuild. There is no dedicated rebuild REST verb, so `rebuild` does what Splunk Web's own Rebuild button does (confirmed against the installed Data Model Manager JS): it POSTs `datamodel/model/<name>` twice, first `acceleration=0` (disable), then `acceleration=1` with the same `acceleration.earliest_time` re-sent explicitly (re-enable).

`rebuild` is only meaningful for an already-accelerated model. If the model's acceleration configuration is disabled, it exits 1 with a clear message before the dry-run or `--yes` guard runs; `--yes` against a non-accelerated model prints no preview and touches nothing.

Because a rebuild is two separate POSTs, a failure between them (for example a permission or connectivity error on the second call) can leave the model disabled without the summary restarting. Splunk Web's Rebuild button carries the same risk; there is no atomic rebuild to fall back to. Run `splunkctl datamodels get <name>` afterwards to confirm `acceleration_enabled` is `true` again.

### Troubleshooting

- `http` with status 503 from `list`: the instance is down or starting; the error envelope carries `kind`, `http_status`, and `message`, never a traceback.
- `not_found` from `get`, `acceleration NAME`, or `rebuild`: the model name is case-sensitive and may live in another app; run `splunkctl datamodels list --filter <text>` and pass `--app`.
- `Data model 'NAME' is not accelerated`: `rebuild` exits 1 and does nothing; enable acceleration in Splunk Web first.
- `percent_complete` stays below 100 after a rebuild: the summarization cron has not caught up; check `last_error` for a peer-level failure before rebuilding again.
- `acceleration_enabled` is `false` after a failed `rebuild --yes`: the second POST failed; fix the `permission` or `connection` error and run `rebuild --yes` again once acceleration is re-enabled in Splunk Web.
- `has_summary: false` with `enabled: true`: acceleration was just enabled; wait for the first cron run.

### See also

- [Manage detection rules](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/rules.md)
- [Run searches](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/search.md)
- [Manage macros, eventtypes, tags](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/knowledge.md)
- [Command reference: datamodels](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/commands/datamodels.md)

## Manage lookups

Source: https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/lookups.md


When to use: a detection needs enrichment from a table you control, such as a threat-intel indicator feed, an asset or identity list, or a GeoIP database, and you need to push the file to a remote instance, keep it current, bind it to a lookup name, and have events enriched automatically at search time.

### Prerequisites

- A profile that passes `splunkctl doctor` including `Web UI reachable`: `upload` and `update` go through the Splunk Web form handler because the REST API requires a server-side path.
- Write access to the target app (`--app`, default `search` for `upload`, `update`, `delete`, and `download`).

### Synopsis

```text
splunkctl lookups list [--app APP] [--filter SUBSTRING] [--limit N] [--offset N]
splunkctl lookups get <NAME> [--app APP]
splunkctl lookups upload <NAME> --file <FILE.csv> [--app APP] [--yes]
splunkctl lookups update <NAME> --file <FILE.csv> [--app APP] [--yes]
splunkctl lookups download <NAME> [--app APP] [--out FILE]
splunkctl lookups delete <NAME> [--app APP] [--yes]
splunkctl lookups definitions [--app APP] [--filter SUBSTRING] [--limit N] [--offset N]
splunkctl lookups define <DEFNAME> (--file <FILE.csv> | --collection <COLLECTION>) [--app APP] [--max-matches N] [--min-matches N] [--case-sensitive|--no-case-sensitive] [--default-match VALUE] [--yes]
splunkctl lookups auto <DEFNAME> --sourcetype <SOURCETYPE> --input <FIELD[:LOOKUP_FIELD]>... --output <FIELD[:RENAMED]>... [--overwrite|--no-overwrite] [--app APP] [--name SUFFIX] [--yes]
```

Uploading a CSV creates a table file on the server, but Splunk does not treat it as a lookup until two more things exist: a lookup definition in `transforms.conf` that binds a name to the file (or, for a KV store collection, to `external_type=kvstore` and `collection=<name>`), which is what `| lookup <defname>` and `| inputlookup <defname>` reference; and optionally an automatic lookup in `props.conf` (`LOOKUP-*`) that wires the definition onto a sourcetype so every matching event is enriched at search time with no `| lookup` in the SPL. `lookups define` writes the first and `lookups auto` the second; both delegate the conf write to the same stanza core that `conf`, `parsers`, and `macros` use.

### Workflow

#### List, inspect, and download

```bash
splunkctl lookups list
splunkctl lookups list --app SA-ThreatIntelligence
splunkctl lookups get threat_indicators.csv
splunkctl lookups download threat_indicators.csv --app SA-ThreatIntelligence --out current_threats.csv
splunkctl lookups definitions
splunkctl lookups definitions --app SA-ThreatIntelligence
```

Expected result: `list` and `get` cover table files across all apps by default; `download` writes the CSV to standard output or `--out`, so you can diff before updating. `definitions` lists only `transforms.conf` stanzas shaped like a lookup definition (a `filename` or `external_type` and `collection` key); `transforms.conf` also holds field-transform stanzas, which `splunkctl conf list transforms` shows unfiltered.

#### Upload or refresh a table file

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host and app in the active profile. Impact: `upload` creates the table file; `update` overwrites the existing file's rows, and every search using it sees the new data at once. Preview with `splunkctl lookups upload threat_indicators.csv --file threat_indicators.csv --app SA-ThreatIntelligence`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl lookups download threat_indicators.csv --app SA-ThreatIntelligence`.

```bash
splunkctl lookups upload threat_indicators.csv --file threat_indicators.csv --app SA-ThreatIntelligence
splunkctl lookups upload threat_indicators.csv --file threat_indicators.csv --app SA-ThreatIntelligence --yes
splunkctl lookups update asset_lookup.csv --file asset_lookup.csv --app SA-IdentityManagement --yes
```

Expected result: the file appears in `splunkctl lookups list --app APP`. The upload goes from your machine through the Splunk Web form handler, the same mechanism the browser uses, so no SSH, SCP, or server filesystem access is needed. Download the current file first when you want a diff.

#### Automate a feed update

```bash
curl -sO https://feeds.example.com/iocs_latest.csv
splunkctl lookups update threat_indicators.csv --file iocs_latest.csv --app SA-ThreatIntelligence --yes
```

Expected result: a lightweight feed pipeline; schedule it with cron or CI after a dry run has been reviewed once. The same safety note as the previous step applies.

#### Define the lookup

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host in the active profile and `transforms.conf` in `--app` (default: current namespace). Impact: the definition `DEFNAME` is created or updated; searches that reference it change behaviour. Preview with `splunkctl lookups define threat_intel --file threat_indicators.csv`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl lookups definitions --filter threat_intel`.

```bash
splunkctl lookups define threat_intel --file threat_indicators.csv
splunkctl lookups define threat_intel --file threat_indicators.csv --yes
splunkctl lookups define asset_intel --collection assets --yes
splunkctl lookups define threat_intel --file threat_indicators.csv --max-matches 1 --case-sensitive --default-match unknown --yes
```

Expected result: `| inputlookup threat_intel` works. `define` requires exactly one of `--file` or `--collection` (otherwise exit 2) and warns, without blocking, when `--file` names a table that does not exist yet in that app, so a scripted define-then-upload flow still works. `--collection` is how a KV store collection becomes queryable (see [Manage KV store collections](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/kvstore.md)). `--max-matches`, `--min-matches`, `--case-sensitive`, and `--default-match` tune how strict the match is and what to emit on a miss.

#### Wire an automatic lookup onto a sourcetype

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host in the active profile and `props.conf` in `--app`. Impact: every event of `--sourcetype` is enriched at search time from now on, which changes field values in existing detections. Preview with `splunkctl lookups auto threat_intel --sourcetype firewall_logs --input dest_ip:ip --output threat_level`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl search oneshot 'sourcetype=firewall_logs | table dest_ip threat_level' --earliest -15m`.

```bash
splunkctl lookups auto threat_intel --sourcetype firewall_logs --input dest_ip:ip --output threat_level --output threat_category
splunkctl lookups auto threat_intel --sourcetype firewall_logs --input dest_ip:ip --output threat_level --output threat_category --yes
splunkctl search oneshot 'sourcetype=firewall_logs | table dest_ip threat_level threat_category'
```

Expected result: events of that sourcetype carry `threat_level` and `threat_category` with no `| lookup` in the search. `--input` and `--output` are repeatable and at least one of each is required (otherwise exit 2). `--input` is `event_field[:lookup_table_field]`: the field you already have, then the lookup column only if it differs. `--output` is `lookup_table_field[:event_field]`: the column you pull in, then what to call it on the event. `--overwrite` (default) emits `OUTPUT`, always overwriting; `--no-overwrite` emits `OUTPUTNEW`, filling only fields the event lacks. `--name` changes the `LOOKUP-` key suffix (default `DEFNAME`). The definition must already exist.

#### Delete a table file

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host and app in the active profile. Impact: the table file is removed and definitions that reference it start failing. Preview with `splunkctl lookups delete old_table.csv --app search`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl lookups list --filter old_table`.

```bash
splunkctl lookups download old_table.csv --out backup/old_table.csv
splunkctl lookups delete old_table.csv --app search
splunkctl lookups delete old_table.csv --app search --yes
```

### Troubleshooting

- `Lookup upload failed` or a `web` error: Splunk Web is not reachable from this machine; check `Web UI reachable` in `splunkctl doctor`.
- `not_found` from `get`, `download`, or `delete`: the file is in another app; `list` spans all apps but `download` and `delete` default to `search`, so pass `--app`.
- `upload` fails because the file exists: use `update` to overwrite.
- A warning from `define` that the table does not exist: upload it with `lookups upload`, or check the filename; the definition was still written.
- Exit 2 from `define` or `auto`: `define` needs exactly one of `--file` or `--collection`; `auto` needs at least one `--input` and one `--output`.
- `| lookup threat_intel` reports an unknown lookup: the definition is in another app or not shared; check `splunkctl lookups definitions --app APP`.
- `permission` from `define` or `auto`: the account cannot write `transforms.conf` or `props.conf` in that app.

### See also

- [Manage KV store collections](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/kvstore.md)
- [Manage source types and extractions](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/parsers.md)
- [Manage detection rules](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/rules.md)
- [Install](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/install.md)
- [Command reference: lookups](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/commands/lookups.md)

## Manage source types and extractions

Source: https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/parsers.md


When to use: you are onboarding a new data source and need a source type in `props.conf`, field extractions in `transforms.conf`, or want those stanzas exported to YAML so they can be reviewed and deployed to another instance.

### Prerequisites

- A Splunk account that can write to the target app (for example the `admin` role, or a role with write access to `search`).
- Source type names are case-sensitive; take the exact spelling from the data input configuration.
- For `import`: a YAML file produced by `parsers export` or written in the same shape.

### Synopsis

```text
splunkctl parsers sourcetypes [--filter SUBSTRING] [--limit N] [--offset N]
splunkctl parsers extractions [--sourcetype SUBSTRING] [--filter SUBSTRING] [--limit N] [--offset N]
splunkctl parsers get <SOURCETYPE> [--conf props|transforms] [--explicit] [--app APP]
splunkctl parsers create --sourcetype <NAME> [--category TEXT] [--transforms TEXT] [--yes]
splunkctl parsers update <SOURCETYPE> [--category TEXT] [--transforms TEXT] [--yes]
splunkctl parsers delete <SOURCETYPE> [--yes]
splunkctl parsers set <STANZA> <KEY=VALUE>... [--conf props|transforms] [--sharing user|app|global] [--create|--no-create] [--yes]
splunkctl parsers unset <STANZA> <KEY>... [--conf props|transforms] [--yes]
splunkctl parsers export --path <FILE.yml> [--conf props|transforms|all] [--filter SUBSTRING]
```
