## Check server health and topology

Source: https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/server.md


When to use: a detection returned nothing and you need to know whether the search ran against a healthy platform, or you are auditing license usage, KV store state, authentication providers, auth tokens, deployment server classes, or workload management on a Splunk instance.

### Prerequisites

- A profile that passes `splunkctl doctor` (see [Configure](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/configure.md)).
- A role that can read `server/` and `cluster/` endpoints; most reads work with `admin`, and the health, license, and KV store views need no cluster membership.
- `tokens` needs Splunk 7.3 or later; `workloads` needs Splunk 8.1 or later with workload management enabled; `serverclasses` and `deployment` need the deployment server enabled.

### Synopsis

```text
splunkctl server health
splunkctl server messages [--dismiss NAME] [--yes]
splunkctl server license [--usage]
splunkctl server kvstore
splunkctl server cluster
splunkctl server shcluster
splunkctl server deployment
splunkctl server search-peers
splunkctl server serverclasses list
splunkctl server serverclasses get <NAME>
splunkctl server serverclasses reload <NAME> [--yes]
splunkctl server tokens list [--user USER]
splunkctl server tokens create --user <USER> [--audience TEXT] [--expires-in DAYS] [--yes]
splunkctl server tokens revoke <TOKEN_ID> [--yes]
splunkctl server auth show
splunkctl server auth ldap
splunkctl server auth saml
splunkctl server auth role-mapping
splunkctl server workloads pools
splunkctl server workloads rules
splunkctl server workloads status
```

Every command accepts the global `--json` flag for machine-readable output.

### Workflow

#### Read the splunkd health report

```bash
splunkctl server health
splunkctl server health --json
```

Expected result: Splunk's health-report tree (search scheduler, disk space, KV store, ingestion latency, and more) flattened to one row per component. Nested feature names join with `/`, and unhealthy components carry their reason text in a `reasons` column. The command reports, it does not gate: red components still exit 0. It complements `doctor` (connectivity-oriented) with splunkd's own self-diagnosis.

#### Triage an empty detection result

```bash
splunkctl server cluster --json
splunkctl server shcluster --json
splunkctl server deployment --json
splunkctl server search-peers
```

Expected result: enough to tell "no threat" (the search ran correctly and nothing matched) from "infrastructure degraded" (an indexer peer is down, the cluster bundle failed to replicate, a forwarder stopped checking in). On a non-clustered instance each command reports a clean disabled or no-clients state and exits 0; that is not an error.

- `cluster`: an overview row (`mode`, `label`, `replication_factor_met`, `search_factor_met`, `rolling_restart`, `maintenance_mode`) followed by one row per peer (`label`, `status`, `site`, `search_state`, `replication_count`, `bucket_count`). When disabled, a single row with `mode: disabled`. Prefers `cluster/manager` (Splunk 9+) and falls back to `cluster/master` on older instances.
- `shcluster`: a captain row (`captain`, `captain_id`, `dynamic_captain`, `elected_captain`) followed by one row per member (`label`, `status`, `site`, `out_of_sync`). When disabled, `mode: disabled`.
- `deployment`: one row per client (`client`, `hostname`, `ip`, `last_phone_home`, `phone_home_interval`), or `status: no_clients, total: 0`.
- `search-peers`: one row per distributed-search peer (`peer`, `status`, `replication_status`, `version`). Empty on a standalone instance.

Genuine REST errors (401, or 503 for reasons other than "not enabled") exit 1 with a classified error envelope.

#### Check license and KV store

```bash
splunkctl server license
splunkctl server license --usage
splunkctl server kvstore
```

Expected result: `license` lists pool usage (used versus quota per pool). `--usage` reports one row with `used`, `quota`, `pct_used` (today's indexed volume against the licensed daily quota), `licenses_valid`, and `soonest_expiry` (earliest expiring non-perpetual license, or `never`). `kvstore` shows status, port, version, and storage engine, with an explicit status word (`ready`, `failed`, `starting`, `unknown`) so a down KV store is never mistaken for a healthy result.

#### Read and dismiss system messages

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host in the active profile. Impact: the message disappears from Splunk Web for every user. Preview with `splunkctl server messages --dismiss warn_disk`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl server messages`.

```bash
splunkctl server messages
splunkctl server messages --dismiss warn_disk --yes
```

Expected result: the list of system messages, then the list without `warn_disk`.

#### Inspect the authentication provider

```bash
splunkctl server auth show
splunkctl server auth ldap
splunkctl server auth saml
splunkctl server auth role-mapping
```

Expected result (all read-only):

- `show`: one row per provider-services entry with `name`, `auth_type` (detected: `Splunk`, `LDAP`, or `SAML`), and `active_authmodule`.
- `ldap`: feature-detects the active auth type first. When LDAP is not configured it returns `{"status": "not_configured", "active_auth": "..."}` and exits 0. When configured it shows `name`, `host`, `port`, `SSLEnabled`, `userBaseDN`, `groupBaseDN`, `bindDN`, `userNameAttribute`, `groupMemberAttribute`.
- `saml`: same detection; when configured it shows `name` (group name) and `roles` (mapped Splunk roles, comma-separated).
- `role-mapping`: every role with `name`, `imported_roles`, `srchFilter`, `srchIndexesAllowed`, `defaultApp`, for auditing which external groups map to which Splunk roles.

#### Manage auth tokens

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host in the active profile. Impact: `create` issues a bearer token that authenticates as `--user` until it expires; `revoke` permanently deletes a token and breaks any automation using it. Preview with `splunkctl server tokens create --user svc --audience my-app --expires-in 30`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl server tokens list --user svc`.

```bash
splunkctl server tokens list
splunkctl server tokens list --user admin
splunkctl server tokens create --user admin --yes
splunkctl server tokens create --user svc --audience my-app --expires-in 30 --yes
splunkctl server tokens revoke <TOKEN_ID> --yes
```

Expected result: `list` shows `id`, `user`, `audience`, `status`, `last_used`, `expires`; tokens that never expire show `never`, unused tokens show `last_used: never`. `create` prints the token value once; save it immediately, it cannot be retrieved later. Omit `--expires-in` for a non-expiring token. Tokens are an alternative to password auth for service accounts and automation.

#### Push apps with deployment server classes

> **Safety:** Target is the deployment server in the active profile. Impact: `reload` pushes the serverclass's current app configuration to every matching forwarder, which may restart splunkd on them when `restartSplunkd` is set. Preview with `splunkctl server serverclasses reload linux_forwarders`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl server deployment` (check `last_phone_home`).

```bash
splunkctl server serverclasses list
splunkctl server serverclasses get linux_forwarders
splunkctl server serverclasses reload linux_forwarders --yes
```

Expected result: `list` shows `name`, `restartSplunkd`, `stateOnClient`, `whitelist`, `blacklist`. `get` adds `repositoryLocation`, `targetRepositoryLocation`, `endpoint`, `filterType`, and an `apps` list (each with `app`, `restartSplunkd`, `stateOnClient`). When the deployment server is not enabled, `list` reports a clean disabled status and exits 0.

#### Review workload management

```bash
splunkctl server workloads pools
splunkctl server workloads rules
splunkctl server workloads status
```

Expected result (read-only): `pools` gives one row per pool (`name`, `cpu_weight`, `mem_weight`, `default_category`, `category`); `rules` one row per admission rule (`name`, `predicate`, `workload_pool`, `action`, `order`, `schedule`); `status` reports `status` (enabled or disabled) and `admission_rules_enabled`, plus a nested `pools` list with `cpu_usage`, `mem_usage`, and `search_count` when pool-level utilisation is available. On older or unconfigured instances each reports a clean not-available status and exits 0.

### Troubleshooting

- `auth` error on every command: credentials are wrong or expired; run `splunkctl doctor`.
- `permission` on `cluster`, `tokens`, or `serverclasses`: the role cannot read that endpoint; use `admin` or add the matching capability.
- `http` 503 on `cluster` or `shcluster` with a reason other than "not enabled": the cluster manager or captain is down; treat detection results from that window as unreliable.
- `not_found` on `tokens revoke`: use the `id` column from `tokens list`, not the token value.
- `not_found` on `messages --dismiss`: the message name is the `name` column from `splunkctl server messages`, not its text.
- `connection` or `timeout`: the management port is unreachable; raise the global `--timeout` or check the network path.

### See also

- [Diagnose a connection](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/doctor.md)
- [Run searches](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/search.md)
- [Manage users and roles](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/users.md)
- [Log in through browser SAML](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/auth.md)
- [Manage KV store collections](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/kvstore.md)
- [Command reference: server](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/commands/server.md)

## Manage KV store collections

Source: https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/kvstore.md


When to use: an allowlist, a threat-intel feed, or an enrichment table lives in Splunk's KV store (schema-less JSON documents scoped per app, the same storage behind Enterprise Security's asset and identity tables) and you need to create the collection, load or query documents, back it up, or remove it.

### Prerequisites

- A profile that passes `splunkctl doctor` with the `KV Store` check at `ready`; `splunkctl server kvstore` shows the status on its own.
- Write access to the target app (`--app`, default `search`); collection ownership is always `nobody`, the KV store convention, so every command addresses `servicesNS/nobody/<app>/storage/collections/{config|data}/...`.
- Every command is a thin, typed wrapper around raw `GET`, `POST`, and `DELETE` calls.

### Synopsis

```text
splunkctl kvstore collections [--app APP]
splunkctl kvstore create <NAME> [--app APP] [--yes]
splunkctl kvstore delete <NAME> [--app APP] [--yes]
splunkctl kvstore query <COLLECTION> [--query JSON] [--limit N] [--skip N] [--sort SPEC] [--app APP]
splunkctl kvstore insert <COLLECTION> (--data JSON | --file DOC.json) [--app APP] [--yes]
splunkctl kvstore update <COLLECTION> <KEY> (--data JSON | --file DOC.json) [--app APP] [--yes]
splunkctl kvstore remove <COLLECTION> [KEY] [--query JSON] [--app APP] [--yes]
splunkctl kvstore export <COLLECTION> [--app APP] [--out FILE.jsonl]
splunkctl kvstore import <COLLECTION> --file <FILE.jsonl> [--app APP] [--yes]
```

### Workflow

#### List collections

```bash
splunkctl kvstore collections
splunkctl kvstore collections --app Splunk_Security_Essentials
```

Expected result: the collection names in the app (default `search`).

#### Create a collection

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host and app in the active profile. Impact: an empty collection is created in that app. Preview with `splunkctl kvstore create ip_allowlist`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl kvstore collections`.

```bash
splunkctl kvstore create ip_allowlist
splunkctl kvstore create ip_allowlist --yes
```

#### Add or replace single documents

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host and app in the active profile. Impact: `insert` adds one document; `update` replaces the whole document stored under `KEY`, not just the fields you pass. Preview with `splunkctl kvstore insert ip_allowlist --data '{"host": "evil.example"}'`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl kvstore query ip_allowlist --query '{"host": "evil.example"}'`.

```bash
splunkctl kvstore insert ip_allowlist --data '{"host": "evil.example"}'
splunkctl kvstore insert ip_allowlist --data '{"host": "evil.example"}' --yes
splunkctl kvstore insert ip_allowlist --file doc.json --yes
splunkctl kvstore update ip_allowlist 64f1c0a2b3d4e5f601234567 --data '{"host": "new.example"}' --yes
```

Expected result: the document is stored unmodified; no field is added, renamed, or stripped. Both commands take exactly one of `--data '<json>'` (inline) or `--file f.json` (a file holding a single JSON object); passing both or neither, or invalid JSON, is a usage error (exit 2).

#### Query documents

```bash
splunkctl kvstore query ip_allowlist
splunkctl kvstore query ip_allowlist --query '{"host": "evil.example"}'
splunkctl kvstore query ip_allowlist --limit 50 --skip 100 --sort '-_key'
```

Expected result: the matching documents, each with its `_key`. `--query` is raw JSON passed unmodified to the API's `query` parameter; `--limit`, `--skip`, and `--sort` map straight to the matching API parameters. There is no client-side re-filtering or re-paging: what the server returns is exactly what is rendered.

#### Remove documents

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host and app in the active profile. Impact: `remove KEY` deletes one document; `remove --query` deletes every document matching the query, with no undo. Preview with `splunkctl kvstore remove ip_allowlist --query '{"host": "evil.example"}'`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl kvstore query ip_allowlist --query '{"host": "evil.example"}'`.

```bash
splunkctl kvstore remove ip_allowlist 64f1c0a2b3d4e5f601234567 --yes
splunkctl kvstore remove ip_allowlist --query '{"host": "evil.example"}'
splunkctl kvstore remove ip_allowlist --query '{"host": "evil.example"}' --yes
```

Exactly one of `KEY` or `--query` is required; supplying both or neither is a usage error (exit 2).

#### Back up and restore with JSONL

```bash
splunkctl kvstore export ip_allowlist
splunkctl kvstore export ip_allowlist --out backup.jsonl
```

Expected result: one JSON document per line on standard output or in the global `--out` file, with `_key` preserved on every line so `import` can upsert straight back onto the same keys.

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host and app in the active profile. Impact: every document in the file is upserted; a document whose `_key` already exists is overwritten. Preview with `splunkctl kvstore import ip_allowlist --file backup.jsonl`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl kvstore query ip_allowlist --limit 5`.

```bash
splunkctl kvstore import ip_allowlist --file ip_allowlist.jsonl
splunkctl kvstore import ip_allowlist --file ip_allowlist.jsonl --yes
```

Expected result: the documents are POSTed through `batch_save` in chunks of up to 500. Overwriting on a matching `_key` is `batch_save`'s own semantics, not something the CLI adds. Blank lines are skipped; any non-blank line that is not a single JSON object is a usage error (exit 2) and the whole import is rejected before any request is sent, never partially applied.

#### Use the collection from SPL

A raw collection name is not usable through `| inputlookup` or `| lookup`: Splunk resolves a lookup definition (a `transforms.conf` stanza with `external_type = kvstore` pointing at the collection), not the collection itself.

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host in the active profile and `transforms.conf` in the current app namespace. Impact: a lookup definition named `ip_allowlist` is created or updated. Preview with `splunkctl lookups define ip_allowlist --collection ip_allowlist`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl search oneshot '| inputlookup ip_allowlist | head 5'`.

```bash
splunkctl lookups define ip_allowlist --collection ip_allowlist --yes
splunkctl search oneshot '| inputlookup ip_allowlist | head 5'
```

See [Manage lookups](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/lookups.md) for automatic lookups onto a sourcetype.

#### Delete a collection

> **Safety:** Target is the Splunk host and app in the active profile. Impact: the collection and all of its documents are removed. Preview with `splunkctl kvstore delete ip_allowlist`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl kvstore collections`.

```bash
splunkctl kvstore export ip_allowlist --out ip_allowlist.jsonl
splunkctl kvstore delete ip_allowlist
splunkctl kvstore delete ip_allowlist --yes
```

Export first so the data can be re-imported.

### Troubleshooting

- `http` with status 503 and `KV Store initialization failed`: the KV store is down; `splunkctl doctor` reports it as `KV Store: failed`. Ask the Splunk admin to restart Splunk or check `mongod.log`. REST failures flow through the error envelope (`kind`, `http_status`, `message`), never a blank result or traceback.
- Exit 2 `exactly one of --data or --file is required` or `exactly one of KEY or --query is required`: pass one source or one target, not both.
- Exit 2 on `import`: a line in the JSONL file is not a single JSON object; fix the file, nothing was sent.
- `not_found` or an empty `query`: the collection is in another app; pass `--app`.
- `| inputlookup NAME` fails in SPL: define the lookup with `splunkctl lookups define NAME --collection NAME --yes`.
- `permission` on `create`, `insert`, or `delete`: the account cannot write to that app.

### See also

- [Manage lookups](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/lookups.md)
- [Check server health and topology](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/server.md)
- [Diagnose a connection](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/doctor.md)
- [Command reference: kvstore](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/commands/kvstore.md)

## Audit changes and attest RBAC

Source: https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/audit.md


When to use: a regulator or reviewer asks who changed a saved search, role, or index and when (`audit changes`), or who holds which capabilities and index access for periodic access recertification (`audit rbac`). Both commands are read-only: no guard, no `--yes`.

### Prerequisites

- A profile that passes `splunkctl doctor` (see [Configure](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/configure.md)).
- For `changes`: search access to `index=_audit` (the `admin` role has it by default).
- For `rbac`: read access to users and roles (`edit_user` and `edit_roles`, or an `admin` account).

### Synopsis

```text
splunkctl audit changes [--since TIME] [--until TIME] [--user USER] [--action SUBSTRING] [--object-type TYPE] [--limit N]
splunkctl audit rbac [--roles-only] [--format csv] [--out FILE]
```

### Workflow

#### Pull the change log for a window

```bash
splunkctl audit changes
splunkctl audit changes --since -7d --until -1d
splunkctl audit changes --limit 2000 --json
```

Expected result: one row per `_audit` event, newest first, with exactly six keys in this order: `time`, `user`, `action`, `object`, `object_type`, `app`. The default window is the last 24 hours (`--since -24h`, `--until now`) and the display cap is 500 rows. Splunk mixes two incompatible event shapes in `_audit`; this command normalizes both:

| Sourcetype | Shape | Mapping |
|---|---|---|
| `audittrail` (legacy) | `Audit:[timestamp=..., user=..., action=..., <tail>]` plain text | `user` and `action` parsed directly; `object` only when the line carries a literal `object="..."` marker (common on capability checks like `edit_user` and `edit_roles`); `object_type` always empty, the legacy format has no per-action type field; `app` from `app="..."` or unquoted `app=...` when present |
| `audittrailv2` (structured) | one JSON object per line | `user` = `actor.name`; `action` = top-level `action`; `object` = `data.name`; `object_type` = `data.type`; `app` = `data.ownership.app` or `data.attributes.app` |

`time` always comes from Splunk's indexed `_time`, not a re-parse of either embedded timestamp, so every row has one consistent, sortable value. Real `audittrailv2` events have no `data.object` or `data.object_type` key; `data.name` and `data.type` are the nearest equivalents and are present on object and system category events (config changes). Action, authn, and check category events (ad-hoc searches, logins, capability grants) carry `data.type` sometimes but rarely `data.name`, so `object` stays empty for them, which is correct: they are not changes to a named object. An event matching neither shape is never dropped; it comes back as `action: "unparsed"` with the full raw line in `object`, so evidence stays complete for formats the parser does not know yet.

#### Filter by user, action, or object type

```bash
splunkctl audit changes --user jdoe
splunkctl audit changes --action edit
splunkctl audit changes --object-type saved_search
splunkctl audit changes --since -30d --user svc_deploy --action edit --format csv --out changes.csv
```

Expected result: only matching rows. `--user` and `--object-type` are case-insensitive exact matches; `--action` is a case-insensitive substring match. Filters run client side on the normalized rows after the fetch, and `--limit` applies after filtering. The raw fetch is unbounded (`count=0`) within the `--since` and `--until` window, so a filter never misses a match because of an arbitrary raw-fetch cutoff. A very wide `--since` over a large `_audit` index fetches every event in that range before limiting, which can be slow; narrow `--since` when you can.

#### Confirm no flag value reaches the SPL

```bash
splunkctl --debug audit changes --user 'x" | delete' --action 'y | outputlookup evil.csv'
```

Expected result: the debug log shows `POST .../search/v2/jobs/ (body: {'search': 'search index=_audit', ...})`. The dispatched search is always the constant `search index=_audit`; `--since` and `--until` go through the job's `earliest_time` and `latest_time` arguments, and the other flags filter rows client side. No flag value, however adversarial, is composed into the SPL string.

#### Export an RBAC recertification report

```bash
splunkctl audit rbac
splunkctl audit rbac --format csv --out recert-2026-07.csv
```

Expected result: one row per user with `user`, `email`, `roles` (direct roles, semicolon-joined), `capabilities`, and `srch_indexes_allowed`. The last two are aggregated across the user's direct roles and the full transitive closure of their imported roles, deduplicated, sorted, and semicolon-joined. Example: role `soc_analyst` imports `power`, which imports `user`; a `soc_analyst` user's effective `capabilities` is the union of all three roles' own capabilities. This is what a role with zero capabilities of its own needs (Splunk's built-in `splunk-system-role` only imports `admin`) to show its real effective grant instead of an empty cell. `rbac` reads roles and users through the SDK only; it dispatches no search.

#### Attest per role instead of per user

```bash
splunkctl audit rbac --roles-only
splunkctl audit rbac --roles-only --format csv --out roles-2026-07.csv
```

Expected result: one row per role with `role`, `imported_roles` (direct only), `capabilities`, and `srch_indexes_allowed`, the last two aggregated the same transitive way, rooted at that role.

Multi-value fields (`roles`, `capabilities`, `srch_indexes_allowed`, `imported_roles`) join with `;`, never a newline. Splunk role, capability, and index names cannot contain a semicolon, so the join is lossless and never produces an embedded newline inside a CSV cell; `--format csv` output round-trips through Python's `csv` module.

### Troubleshooting

- `permission` or an empty result from `changes`: your role cannot search `index=_audit`; use an `admin` account or add `_audit` to the role's allowed indexes.
- `timeout` on `changes`: the window is too wide; narrow `--since` or raise the global `--timeout`.
- Rows show `action: "unparsed"`: the event matched neither audit shape; the raw line is in `object`, so the evidence is still complete.
- `object_type` is empty on every row: the instance writes only the legacy `audittrail` shape, which has no type field; filter on `--action` instead.
- `permission` from `rbac`: the account cannot list users or roles; it needs `edit_user` and `edit_roles` or an `admin` role.
- Fewer rows than expected: `--limit` defaults to 500 after filtering; raise it.

### See also

- [Manage users and roles](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/users.md)
- [Run searches](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/search.md)
- [Exit codes](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/exit-codes.md)
- [Command reference: audit](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/commands/audit.md)

## Administer SOAR users and roles

Source: https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/soar-admin.md


When to use: you need to create or deactivate a SOAR user, rotate a password, change role membership, provision an automation account, review the built-in role permission matrix, or pull the platform audit trail for a user, container, playbook, or time range.

### Prerequisites

- SOAR credentials in the active profile and a passing `splunkctl soar test` (see [Set up and check SOAR](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/soar.md)).
- An account whose role may manage users and roles (the built-in Administrator role does).
- Role names from `splunkctl soar roles list`.

### Synopsis

```text
splunkctl soar users list [--type normal|automation]
splunkctl soar users get <USER_ID>
splunkctl soar users create --username <NAME> [--password TEXT] [--type normal|automation] [--role ROLE]... [--allowed-ip IP]... [--first-name TEXT] [--last-name TEXT] [--yes]
splunkctl soar users update <USER_ID> [--password TEXT] [--add-role ROLE]... [--remove-role ROLE]... [--first-name TEXT] [--last-name TEXT] [--allowed-ip IP]... [--yes]
splunkctl soar users delete <USER_ID> [--yes]
splunkctl soar users token <USER_ID>

splunkctl soar roles list
splunkctl soar roles get <ROLE_ID>

splunkctl soar audit [--user NAME] [--container CONTAINER_ID] [--playbook NAME] [--start ISO8601] [--end ISO8601] [--format csv] [--limit N]
```

### Workflow

#### List and inspect users

```bash
splunkctl soar users list
splunkctl soar users list --type normal
splunkctl soar users list --type automation --json
splunkctl soar users get 5
splunkctl soar users token 5
```

Expected result: one row per user. The system `automation` user is hidden from `/rest/ph_user` by default; `--type automation` surfaces it, `--type normal` shows human users only. `token` shows the hashed key and expiry date for a user, which is explicitly not the usable plaintext token.

#### Create a user

> **Safety:** Target is the SOAR host in the active profile. Impact: a new account that can log in (or call the REST API, for `--type automation`) with the roles you grant. Preview with `splunkctl soar users create --username analyst1 --type normal --role Analyst`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl soar users list`.

```bash
splunkctl soar users create \
    --username analyst1 --password 'P@ss!' \
    --type normal --role Analyst --yes
splunkctl soar users create \
    --username bot_user \
    --password 'StrongP@ss1' \
    --type automation \
    --role Automation \
    --allowed-ip 10.0.0.1 \
    --yes
```

Expected result: the user exists with the given roles and, for automation users, the allowed IPs. Omit `--password` to be prompted securely; the preview masks it as `********`. For automation users the CLI prints a notice: the automation token plaintext is shown once in the SOAR UI at creation time and cannot be retrieved through REST (`users token` returns only the hashed key).

#### Update a user

> **Safety:** Target is the SOAR host in the active profile. Impact: the password, roles, profile fields, or allowed IPs change for that account immediately. Preview with `splunkctl soar users update 5 --add-role Observer --remove-role Analyst`, apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl soar users get 5`.

```bash
splunkctl soar users update 5 --password 'NewP@ss!' --yes
splunkctl soar users update 5 \
    --add-role Observer \
    --remove-role Analyst \
    --first-name Jane \
    --yes
splunkctl soar users update 7 --allowed-ip 10.0.0.1 --allowed-ip 10.0.0.2 --yes
```

Expected result: roles use a read-modify-write pattern: `--add-role` and `--remove-role` fetch the current role list, merge the change, and post the result. `--allowed-ip` replaces the whole list. Passwords are masked in the dry-run preview.

#### Deactivate a user

> **Safety:** Target is the SOAR host in the active profile. Impact: SOAR user deletion is a soft delete (`is_active=False`); the record stays, logins stop, and the user's automation token returns "User is inactive" on every later API call. Preview with `splunkctl soar users delete 5` (the preview explains the soft delete), apply by adding `--yes`, and verify with `splunkctl soar users get 5`.

```bash
splunkctl soar users delete 5
splunkctl soar users delete 5 --yes
```

#### Review roles

```bash
splunkctl soar roles list
splunkctl soar roles list --json | jq '.[].name'
splunkctl soar roles get 1
```

Expected result: SOAR ships with 7 immutable built-in roles; `list` shows the full permission matrix and `get` shows one role in detail. Use the names here for `--role`, `--add-role`, and `--remove-role`.

#### Query the audit log

```bash
splunkctl soar audit
splunkctl soar audit --user admin
splunkctl soar audit --container 42
splunkctl soar audit --playbook dns_lookup
splunkctl soar audit --start 2026-01-01 --end 2026-06-30
splunkctl soar audit --user admin --start 2026-07-01 --limit 100
splunkctl soar audit --format csv
```

Expected result: audit rows filtered by user, container, playbook, or time range (`--start` and `--end` are ISO 8601). The endpoint returns a bare array, which the CLI normalizes like every other list. `--format csv` asks the server for CSV; `--limit` caps the rows.

### Troubleshooting

- `permission` on `users` or `roles`: the account's role cannot manage users; use an Administrator account or token.
- `not_found` on `users get`, `update`, or `delete`: commands take the numeric id from `splunkctl soar users list`, not the username.
- `http` 400 on `create` or `update`: the server rejected a field; check that each `--role` matches a name from `splunkctl soar roles list` and read the message for the failing field.
- `auth` error from an automation user after `delete`: expected, the account is inactive; create a new one, the token cannot be revived.
- The automation token is not in any output: by design; copy it from the SOAR UI at creation. `users token` only confirms the hash and expiry.
- `--start` rejected: use ISO 8601 (`2026-07-01` or `2026-07-01T00:00:00`).

## Exit codes

Source: https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/exit-codes.md


When to use: you are writing a shell script, CI step, or agent wrapper around splunkctl and need to branch on `$?` to distinguish success, operational errors, and bad invocations.

| Code | Meaning | Examples |
|------|---------|---------|
| 0 | Success | Command completed normally. |
| 1 | Command error | Auth failure, resource not found, API/network error, validation rejected by the server, runtime fault. |
| 2 | Usage error | Invalid argument, unknown option, missing required option, unrecognized subcommand. |

### Details

**Code 0**: the command ran and produced its result. For mutation commands with `--yes`, the change was applied. For dry-run previews (the default), the preview was printed successfully.

**Code 1**: the command understood what you asked for but could not complete it. Common causes:

- Write SPL refused without `--yes` (`confirmation_required` in JSON errors).
- Authentication or authorization failure (wrong credentials, expired token, insufficient role): `auth` or `permission`.
- Resource not found (no such index, saved search, dashboard, lookup, container, playbook): `not_found`.
- Server-side validation error (invalid cron, duplicate name, field constraint): `conflict` or `http`.
- Network or connectivity error (host unreachable, timeout, TLS handshake failure): `connection` or `timeout`.
- Unreadable or foreign config file: `config`.

With `--json`, the error is a single-line envelope on standard output: `{"error": {"kind": "...", "http_status": ..., "message": "..."}}`.

**Code 2**: Click rejected the invocation before the command ran. The arguments or options did not match the command's schema. Fix the invocation and retry. This code is never produced by splunkctl's own logic; it comes from the argument parser. Commands that validate mutually exclusive options themselves (for example `kvstore insert --data` versus `--file`) also raise a usage error and exit 2.

### Scripting example

```bash
splunkctl rules list --format json > rules.json
case $? in
  0) echo "OK";;
  1) echo "command failed" >&2; exit 1;;
  2) echo "bad usage" >&2; exit 2;;
esac
```

## Relationship to Splunk's splunkctl

Source: https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/splunk-cli.md


This project started in June 2026. In August 2026 Splunk Inc. published an unrelated, experimental Go CLI with the same name at [`splunk/splunkctl`](https://github.com/splunk/splunkctl). The two tools share a name and nothing else. This project is not a fork, wrapper, or replacement for Splunk's tool, and it focuses on SOC workflows across Splunk Enterprise, Enterprise Security, and Splunk SOAR rather than on general Splunk administration.

### Comparison

| | This project (`pip install splunkctl`) | `splunk/splunkctl` |
|---|---|---|
| Language and install | Python package from PyPI | Go binary from GitHub Releases |
| Products | Splunk Enterprise, Enterprise Security, Splunk SOAR | Splunk Enterprise, Splunk Cloud Platform |
| Authentication | Username and password by default, bearer token, optional browser SAML SSO | Bearer token only |
| Profiles | Named profiles for dev, UAT, and production | One host and token |
| Mutations | Dry run by default, `--yes` to apply | Prompt, or `CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED` for non-interactive callers; `--read-only` |
| AI agents | Built-in MCP server plus `commands --json` | `schema` JSON and agent skill files; pairs with Splunk's MCP server |
| Configuration as code | `state pull`, `diff`, and `push` with change reports | Not provided |
| Command surface | SOC-focused groups (see the [command reference](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/commands/README.md)) | Generated from Splunk's REST definitions, including cluster and licenser internals |
| Config file | `~/.splunkctl/config.yaml` with profiles | `~/.splunkctl/config.yaml` with flat `host` and `token` keys |
| Support | Community project, Apache-2.0 | Experimental, Apache-2.0, pull requests not accepted |

Both tools install an executable named `splunkctl` and read the same configuration path.

### Coexistence

- **Executable name.** This package installs both `splunkctl` and `splunkctl-py`. If Splunk's binary shadows `splunkctl` on your `PATH`, call `splunkctl-py` instead.
- **Config file.** If `~/.splunkctl/config.yaml` holds Splunk's flat `host`/`token` format, this tool leaves it untouched and keeps its own profiles in `~/.splunkctl/profiles.yaml`. It prints one notice on standard error when that happens, and `splunkctl doctor` reports which file is in use. Pass `--config FILE` to choose a file explicitly; an explicit file in Splunk's format is refused rather than redirected.
- **Credentials are not shared.** The two tools do not read each other's settings. Run `splunkctl config init` once to set up this tool.

### Check which tool you are running

```bash
splunkctl --version
```

This project prints `splunkctl, version X.Y.Z`. If the output looks different, `splunkctl` on your `PATH` is Splunk's binary; use `splunkctl-py`.

- [Configure](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/configure.md)
- [Diagnose a connection](https://splunkctl.danny.vn/guides/doctor.md)
